item.title: Navigating Emotional Expression in Asian American Parenting
item.description:
Parenting

Navigating Emotional Expression in Asian American Parenting

Cultural mismatches can obscure immigrant parents' best intentions and efforts.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Emotions tend to be expressed more verbally in the U.S. compared to many non-Western societies.
  • Many immigrant Asian American parents express affection through nonverbal acts of care and sacrifice.
  • Acculturative mismatches can lead children to misinterpret implicitly caring parents as unloving.
Source: wangbinghua/Unsplash

Since 2015, Pixar’s Inside Out movies have been lauded for promoting emotional literacy among children and caregivers alike. The films anthropomorphize the “basic emotions,” naming and bringing such feelings to life as colorful characters. They go beyond extolling the American pursuit of happiness to normalize people’s natural ranges of emotions, including sadness and anxiety.

Within the history of emotions, this multi-billion dollar-grossing series can be seen as a product of a broader U.S. trend toward emotional expression. Americans’ use of emotional vocabulary has increased since the 1960s, thanks to the growing presence of psychology and popular media. U.S. parenting books emphasize teaching children to label their feelings. Yet, it seems less clear whether this expressiveness has expanded in all U.S. subcommunities.

In particular, the Asian American population has also grown since the 1960s, from 0.6 percent to now over 7 percent of Americans, largely due to immigration. This has created households with acculturative gaps. Different generations within Asian American families may experience cultural divides far wider than those broadly between Boomers and Millennials, or Gen X caregivers and Gen Alpha youth. Many differences center on norms of communication. Verbally explicit emotionality, like that of Inside Out, may feel less familiar to many first-generation Asian American parents. Promoting parental understanding and intentional navigation of this normative mismatch may support household harmony, wellbeing, and parent-child connection.

Mapping out mismatches

As a psychiatrist, I worked with a first-generation Korean American father with somatic symptoms. He once recounted his surprise, not long after immigrating decades ago—but long before Inside Out was imaginable—at a U.S. movie character saying the words “You hurt me.” This devoted father was in no way deficient in emotions, despite his outward restraint, but had adopted a bicultural identity not entirely aligned with the U.S. “low-context culture.” Hierarchical relational contexts and nonverbal actions still mattered to him; communicating entirely through explicit words did not feel proper. When he felt unfairly treated at work, rather than directly confronting his boss, he would silently reduce his commitment or simply leave.

This father’s “high-context” expression style resonated to varying extents as I worked with some other Asian American parents. All of them were first-generation immigrants; hardly surprising, as over two-thirds of Asian American adults were born outside the U.S. Moreover, they consistently showed good intentions for their children. When I worked with their children as well, familial discord most often seemed to result from unrealized, intergenerational acculturative mismatches. Habits completely adaptive in their ancestral countries no longer had the same effect in America; what drove generations apart was certainly not any innate inferiority of either culture, but their cross-cultural dissonance.

Does parental devotion have to involve explicitly verbal validation and articulating feelings? Collectivistic norms of emotional restraint may reflexively channel parental affection towards nonverbal, instrumental acts of care and sacrifice. Many immigrant parents will not hesitate to spend hard-earned money on children’s educations and futures, whether on tuition, tutoring, or supplementary courses, sometimes into their children’s adulthood. Hours devoted to quality home cooking may reflect real affection, comfort-giving, and teaching children their heritage on a viscerally memorable level. Accompanying and paying for violin lessons, traditional dance classes, and weekend language schooling might be intended to instill positive long-term qualities into children, even if caregivers do not verbalize that.

Herein lie the origins of many intergenerational misunderstandings and misassumptions. Between the private sphere of home and the public sphere of school, gatherings, and work, Asian American parents and children often navigate emotional regimes with highly distinct standards for affective expression. For many Asian American children who see friends copiously praised by teachers or their parents, they may wonder why this does not happen as much at home. Having internalized Anglo-American culture through socialization and media, some youth assume a parental lack of emotional vocabulary means a lack of emotional depth, warmth, or care. Conversely, parents at least initially may not see this alternative perspective, even if they have tried to acculturate.

Why is my teenager so ungrateful, resentful, and rejecting of our heritage, despite my devotion to them?

Comparative development

A developmental perspective can partly explain acculturative gaps between Asian American parents and children. Both could settle as first-generation immigrants, whether a 30-year-old father with a 3-year-old, or a 40-year-old mother with a 14-year-old, and still diverge deeply in their cultural identities over time. People who immigrate as grown adults have largely achieved identity formation and, moreover, understand their culture of origin with nuance. Those raised only in the U.S. lack such lived knowledge and may, if frequently otherized, unknowingly develop internalized racism.

Unaddressed exclusion due to outward differences—one’s pronunciation of certain words, mannerisms, or even food brought from home—has distinct potential consequences in each phase of development. A community’s diversity may influence the likelihood of such experiences. A 6-year-old unable to fit into peer groups may develop long-term feelings of inferiority and incompetence. A 16-year-old who prioritizes peer relations more than before could, if judged for being neither “American enough” nor “Asian enough,” lack a stable, grounded identity and chronically question themselves. In contrast, a fully grown immigrant parent might not experience so deep an impact on their self-concept.

Asian American youth typically must explore where they want to be on a bicultural spectrum of identity. If facing perceived social failure and trying to gain peer acceptance, some minoritized youth reject their own heritage, finding it embarrassing or even contemptible. If taken far enough, this blame might extend to associating Asian-ness with lack of emotional depth and personality; they may interpret their parents’ normative expression styles as “proof” in a confirmation bias. Here, mutually making sense of the intergenerational mismatch is far more productive than blaming either parent or child.

Informed navigation

Parenting norms vary across Asian American subgroups and within communities themselves. “1.5th,” second, and third-generation parents may feel relatively less of a normative divide with their children, even if they occupy different locations along a biculturality spectrum. First-generation immigrant parents may especially benefit from explicit explanations of why acculturative gaps exist with their children. Such education would do well to identify normative differences in emotional communication that are not readily obvious. From there, parents can incorporate such insights into interactions with their children. At minimum, this can reduce blame over mismatches.

A key question is how to extend such education to immigrant families. Concise resources about U.S. communication norms could be made multilingually accessible to immigrant parents at schools, pediatric offices, and community centers. Outreach efforts could enlist community health workers, social workers, and cultural brokers. Moreover, immigrant epistemic trust is not always high toward psychiatrists and therapists, but culturally concordant mental health professionals can be well-suited to invite and uncover psychosocial fault lines with struggling immigrant parents. Beyond individual therapy, cultural humility-informed family therapies, like that of CHATogether, can improve parent-child perspective-taking and emotional communication.

Asian American parents do not have to forego their heritage, practice inauthenticity, or adopt every emotional norm from Inside Out. Rather, teaching parents about comparative norms of emotionality can inform how exactly they want to acculturate and navigate complex dynamics with their children. Bridging the disconnect between how affection is expressed and recognized could bring many immigrant families much closer together.

item.title: There Will Never Be Another "Tom Sawyer"
item.description:
Media

There Will Never Be Another "Tom Sawyer"

Personal Perspective: As we gain access to everything, we share less. We are losing our glue.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Mass communication created a brief window when humanity could share the same songs, films, and icons.
  • Infinite digital choice has fragmented us into isolated bubbles without common culture.
  • Because the old unity was accidental, rebuilding connection now requires that we choose it deliberately.

I was watching a YouTube video the other night, Drumeo's "The Genius of Rush's Tom Sawyer." The host, Brandon Toews, clearly poured himself into it. He, along with a handful of fellow drummers and musicians, took turns reverently breaking down what Neil Peart, Rush's incomparable drummer, did on that track. The way the song breathes and then detonates. It is a defiant, transcendent anthem of individuality. Watching it, I felt that thing Rush fans know. There's a reason we recognize each other.

We're a particular kind of nerd, if that's even the right word. We appreciate the complexity, the virtuosity, and the crafted brilliance of Geddy Lee, Alex Lifeson, and Neil Peart. Every fan knows the cerebral spirituality of Neil's lyrics. He didn't write fluffy love songs. He wrote about consciousness, time, and free will. He sought deep truths and shared them in mystic rhythms.

Neil was an atheist. He was also one of my greatest spiritual teachers. Rush fans reading this know exactly what I mean.

I have tickets to see Rush in Fort Worth on June 26th with my best buddies. So, fair warning: This isn't neutral. The love of Rush, for me, is closer to the heart.

But sitting there watching that Drumeo video, something hit me that goes way past Rush. Brandon was gushing about what a classic "Tom Sawyer" is, and it triggered a thought that landed with a force of clarity. We will never have another song like this. We will never have another band like this. And it isn't because the talent is gone. It's because the conditions are gone. The window has closed.

The Shared Culture Curve

Let me back up. Way up.

For most of human existence, we lived in small hunter-gatherer tribes of 50 to 150 people. For the most part, our tribes existed separately from one another. We were nomads with different valleys, gods, songs, and stories. We were all the same but sitting around different fires.

article continues after advertisement

Eventually, civilization began with the agricultural revolution, and the industrial revolution gave us mass communication. The printing press spread words through books and newspapers. Then we learned to transmit them electronically: telegraph, telephone, radio, film, television, the internet. For the first time in 300,000 years, we could share stories at scale, in the blink of an eye.

Here's the part nobody talks about. There was a window where we had enough bandwidth to share and not yet enough options to fragment. A supply-and-demand sweet spot. We had television and then cable, but still limited options. We had top-40 radio and MTV, when they still played music.

In that window, shared culture exploded with shared icons: Elvis, the Beatles, Michael Jackson, Madonna, U2, "Star Wars," "Raiders of the Lost Ark," and so on. In a sense, they were pioneers, our shared archetypes.

They weren't just talented people and great works of art. They emerged from a synchronicity of conditions, a moment when humanity needed someone to fill the archetype, with the channels to broadcast them to all of us at once. We knew them together. We loved them together. We mourned them together. The shared songs and stories not only made us—they connected us. The icons became a stadium we all walked into together.

We didn't have access to everything, everywhere, all at once. We forgot the cautionary tale: Be careful what you wish for. Our "Monkey's Paw" wish came true. We should have known that what makes something precious isn't abundance. It's scarcity. We've fragmented into division without the shared songs and stories to hold us together.

Mass media created a brief sweet spot where we had enough access to connect but few enough options to share the same songs and stories. Digital abundance then gave us access to everything while we shared almost nothing (a conceptual model illustrating the post's thesis, not measured data).
Source: Mike Brooks, AI-generated with DALL-E / OpenAI

The Other Side of the Curve

We all carry smartphones with access to essentially infinite content, curated for us by algorithms owned by Big Money. Every one of us in our own personalized bubble, recommended our own micro-icons that come and go. The same technology that finally let us share everything has fractured us into tiny shards of glass.

When was the last time a song came out that everyone learned the words to? Not just "everyone in your feed," but nearly everyone. Who's the last musician both your grandmother and your teenage nephew could sing along to?

Here's the part that struck me hardest. It's not just that we don't have new icons. It's that we can't have new icons of that magnitude, because the archetypes have all been claimed.

article continues after advertisement

Imagine a rock band pioneering a new genre without being compared to something else. It would be like trying to invent a completely new style of painting. The low-hanging fruit has all been picked. Christopher Columbus didn't find the New World because he was uniquely brilliant. He found it because he was there first, when there was still a continent left to find. There will be no second Columbus. We can't break ground a second time.

That's where we are with shared culture. There will be no second Beatles. There will be no second "Tom Sawyer." (And yes, luck and timing always mattered. As Malcolm Gladwell argued in Outliers, the icons we got were never the only ones who could have filled those slots. But now the window itself has closed.)

Exhibit A: DeWayne and Me

Source: Mike Brooks/original

Let me make this concrete. One of my best friends since we were six years old is named DeWayne. Coincidentally, we became friends about the same time Rush formed as a band. We grew up together in the suburbs of Houston. We loved Rush’s song “Subdivisions” because we lived it.

Our first concert ever was The Police, on the Synchronicity tour. I'm not making that up. Perhaps the universe, or God, winks at us sometimes. Our second was Rush, headlining the Texas Jam at the Astrodome on the Grace Under Pressure tour. We've been to a number of Rush shows together over the decades. DeWayne’s the one who got us the tickets to Fort Worth.

DeWayne and I are on opposite sides of the political fence, and have been for a while. In the current climate, that should be enough to end a friendship. Our shared love of Rush is part of why it didn't. I love him for who he is, not for who I want him to be. Fifty years of friendship transcends tribalism. Beneath everything that's supposed to divide us is what Neil called the real relation, the underlying theme: our shared love of a band, and of each other, that holds no matter what else is happening in the country.

article continues after advertisement

That's shared culture doing its job. That's what being in the stadium feels like. That's neighbors staying neighbors when politics tries to make us enemies. We’re all in the same stadium -together.

This isn’t theory. It’s needed for our very survival. Despite our differences, DeWayne and I know that we are in the same stadium. Rush reminds us of that.

The Garage

I should tell you why this hits me so hard right now. Neil died in January 2020. The Covid-19 pandemic came two months later. I had to shut down my group psychology practice. The gym is my therapy, and the gyms closed.

What I had left was a small space in a crowded suburban garage: a JBL speaker, a weight set, and a heavy bag. That became my fortress of solitude. What played in it, hour after hour, was Rush. They weren't only my therapy. They were my sanity.

I went through the entire catalog, album by album, building my ultimate Rush playlist and discovering new favorites. The music, and Neil's lyrics, kept me free from the prison of a pandemic. Even alone in that garage, when I felt so small, Rush helped me to dream big. That's what shared culture does at its best: it reminds you that you're not alone.

The Color of Right

For decades I've watched, increasingly alarmed and saddened, as America devolves into hateful political tribalism. Every time I think it can't get any worse, it does. Even a pandemic couldn't unite us.

In that garage, one Rush song in particular became my new favorite. A deep cut from Test for Echo called "The Color of Right." The chorus, and then its variation:

"I am so full of what is right, I can't see what is good."

"I am so full of what is right, I can't see what is true."

I sat with that lyric and felt something about a song I hadn't felt before. Neil had diagnosed what was wrong with our entire world, in a song, in 1996, decades before social media, echo chambers, and filter bubbles. Our certainty about what is right blinds us to what is good and true.

article continues after advertisement

I'm a clinical psychologist. I make diagnoses for a living, and I know one when I see one. What is a diagnosis but the truth of what is wrong?

Why This Is Existential

Here's where I stop being a Rush fan and flip back to being a psychologist. The bell curve of shared culture isn't a music problem. It's an existential one.

Humans are story-making creatures. Shared stories are essential to our survival. We bond through shared narrative: the songs, films, jokes, and references we all get. Shared culture is the connective tissue that lets a species this size cooperate at all. Strip it away and we don't get freedom. We divide into tribalism. Eight billion strangers with no common stories left to remind us we're the same species. Neil saw the danger of carving the world into territories and pulling for our own little tribe. We forget we're all neighbors in an interconnected world.

Look around. We are not replacing shared culture with better shared culture. We are replacing it with tribal identities and disposable micro-icons that flash for thirty-six hours and vanish. We've become a mile wide and an inch deep. We are drowning in the shallows. The shared culture that once helped us bridge our divides is gone, and the arrow only flies forward, at an accelerating rate.

The Truth Tom Sawyer Knew

Here's where replaying Rush endlessly through a pandemic produced an epiphany. Despite hearing "Tom Sawyer" a million times and knowing the lyrics by heart, one line struck me like a thunderbolt. Halfway through the song, Neil writes:

"Changes aren't permanent. But change is."

Read it twice. Give it space to breathe.

What we built—the icons, the achievements, the shared cultural moments—was never permanent. It was a window: the specific shape of connection we had between roughly 1955 and 2005. Nothing gold can stay.

But change itself is permanent. It's the only thing that is. And even change changes. We now have artificial intelligence (AI), and the pace of change is itself accelerating beyond our biological capacity to adapt. Not only can't we go back to simpler times, but the future is also arriving faster than ever.

What Comes Next

The old shared culture happened to us. It was organic and accidental, a gift of timing we didn't engineer and can't reverse-engineer. We can't sit around waiting for the next Beatles to unite us by accident, because the conditions that made accidental unity possible are gone.

So if we want connective tissue now, we have to choose it on purpose. The way DeWayne and I choose it, across a canyon that's supposed to make us enemies. That kind of connection used to be handed to us by the culture. Now we build it ourselves, one person at a time. That isn't a downgrade. It might be the most important thing we ever learn to do.

To keep change from tearing us apart, we have to choose. Fittingly, Neil wrote about that too. "I will choose a path that's clear," he sang. "I will choose free will"

How do we use our free will? How about we choose to remember that we’re all neighbors in the same stadium?

Dedication: Neil Peart said he never wanted to be famous. He only wanted to be great at something he loved and to inspire others. Professor, you did. Not only is this post proof, but also my entire life is better because of Rush.

item.title: Why Today’s Young Professionals Need More Grit
item.description:
Career

Why Today’s Young Professionals Need More Grit

To succeed in today's workforce, it takes more than talent.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Today’s world of work requires the ability to navigate change, uncertainty, and adversity.
  • Young professionals need to develop their soft skills if they want to be successful.
  • Grit means using one’s strengths and developing weaknesses in pursuit of a goal.
Source: Campaign Creators / Unsplash

My university’s graduation ceremony, like schools across the country, was filled with the usual sort of platitudes: Go after your dreams, be courageous, do something bigger than yourself, don’t shrink in the face of adversity, and so on. All great thoughts and what graduates and their family members needed to hear in that moment of celebration.

They should also know that what comes after will be a lot of hard work, uncertainty, and, yes—adversity. The job market is tough and likely getting tougher. The world, and the world of work, is shifting underneath our feet as we speak, and we don’t know where it will be in a year, five years, or more. Lots of organizations are pulling back from hiring, especially new graduates and other young professionals.

When I speak to college seniors, I like to share research from today’s hiring managers that examines their concerns about new hires. More than half say recent grads are unprepared for the workforce and are difficult to manage. Sixty-five percent say they had to fire at least one recent college graduate within the past year (Resume, 2025).

The reactions from students are typically mixed, ranging from shock to acceptance to wanting to argue the point. What I always tell them is this: The frustrations that today’s older adults have with the younger ones are nothing new. The same things were said about my generation and will continue to be said about the next. This is the nature of generations mixing in the workforce.

And, whether true or not, perception is reality. If you are surrounded by people who believe young people have no work ethic, lack motivation, are entitled, have a bad attitude, and are unprepared for work, then it’s your job to prove those people wrong.

Recently I heard an HR leader say, “Young people today need more grit.” And I think that’s true. The job market has been hard before, and navigating work as a new grad has always been challenging. But there’s something different about what’s happening today, due to the headwinds of AI, layoffs, and downsizing, not to mention still-lingering impacts of the pandemic.

Today’s young professionals, if they want to be successful, are going to need to get a little gritty, in addition to that degree they just earned. Today's employee is measured not on potential, but on the ability to navigate uncertainty, make an impact, and work through adversity with a high-level of professionalism from day one. And while that may seem unfair, the good news is, for most fields, it's the soft skills that will help you stand out in this environment. And those are skills you can develop.

The Power of Soft Skills

In any list of competencies that today's employers are looking for, you'll see some combination of problem-solving, initiative, resilience, flexibility, agility, creativity, self-awareness, and communication skills alongside the need for technical and AI fluency (Future, 2025; Job Outlook, 2025). And while "grit" does not explicitly appear on these lists, it underlies them, as employers are no longer willing to teach these skills to new professionals. They're expecting the employee to show up ready to contribute on day one, and willing and able to acquire the skills and knowledge they need on their own. If you want to succeed in today's workforce, if you want to get ahead, you simply cannot do it without grit.

Grit, a term made popular by psychologist Angela Duckworth, is essentially having the qualities of persistence and perseverance to sustain effort toward a goal. More specifically, “achievement is the product of talent and effort, the latter a function of the intensity, direction, and duration of one’s exertions toward a goal” (Duckworth et al., 2007). It’s not enough to be talented, smart, or focused to be successful, in other words. It’s talent and effort, and the ability and willingness to sustain that effort over time. Grittiness may not be mentioned nor measured by the hiring manager, but your ability to pursue your goals in the face of uncertainty, adversity, and a rapidly changing world of work is key to your success.

How Do You Do It?

Unfortunately, telling someone to “get gritty” doesn’t exactly lead to clearly defined behaviors at work or anywhere else. Here is where I would like all young people to start.

  • Know your strengths and lean into them. Figure out what you’re good at and how to capitalize on those things where you are. If you’re great at working in teams, find projects that let you do that. If you have strong analytical skills, raise your hand for those projects. Being gritty means not waiting for someone to put your strengths to work. It's finding places where you can contribute to support the organization and your team's success.
  • Know your weaknesses and develop a plan to address them. Everyone has things they don’t do well. And just because you aren’t good at something doesn’t mean you don’t have to do it, especially when it comes to work. This is what working through adversity and challenge is all about. The gritty professional is the one who acknowledges their learning and ability gaps, and seeks out opportunities to grow in those areas, without having to be told to do so.
  • Get and stay educated. In today’s world of work, the most successful people are those who are lifelong learners. Get educated on your role, organization, and industry. Know what’s happening with the job market, AI, the economy, and other factors that may have direct impact on you. There is no excuse for not having knowledge today. Make “being a learner” one of your top strengths.
  • Set and work toward your goals. Today’s workplace has little time or patience to help you figure out where you need to be. If your manager doesn’t provide goals for your work, then set them for yourself. Think in 30-60-90 day increments and set goals for how you would like this role to connect to your longer-term career plan. Share these with your manager to make them part of the process. But don’t sit back and wait for someone to tell you what to do. They won’t.
  • Know the difference between failure and mistakes. Everyone makes mistakes, and you need to get ready to make a lot of them. What matters is not whether you’re messing something up; it’s how you react to it and what you do with that information moving forward. A gritty person uses setbacks as learning opportunities, fixes their mistakes, and moves forward. And yes, you may fail at some point. But most things in life that seem like failures are just mistakes. Learn to spot the difference.
  • Find your people. Finally, always remember that even in this high-tech, AI-run world, we are all only as good as the people with whom we surround ourselves. Build relationships with your co-workers, with mentors and sponsors, and with your community. Your skills and your relentless pursuit of your goals can only get you so far. Your people are the ones who will open doors for you, give you the feedback you need along the way, and stand in your corner when others won’t. Be as gritty about building relationships as you are about the work.

item.title: Sportsmanship and Young Children
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Sportsmanship and Young Children

Who is watching, who is playing, and does it matter for sportsmanship?

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Children are actively developing attitudes about winning and losing based on what they see and hear.
  • Sportsmanship is the ethical environment that keeps the game fair.
  • Sports can be a great physical outlet and learning opportunity for young children.
  • The onus is on the adults to make sure that the life-lesson learning experience happens.

Sam went with his dad and grandma to a local college’s season-ending basketball game. Sam had just started shooting the ball in his child-sized driveway “court” with his dad and was excited to watch “large people” play the game. With minutes to go in a close game, a player missed a free throw and a cheer went up on the far side of the court. Sam, bewildered, turned to his grandma and asked, “Why are people cheering when he missed? Isn’t that the wrong time to cheer?” He was just learning the rules of the game, but he knew something was off. A sportsmanship teachable moment for sure.

The sidelines and bleachers of our playing fields are the boot camps of sportsmanship. Family members, coaches, and referees staff that boot camp, while the kids play, wait on the bench and run around soaking up lessons in rule-following, breaking, or bending. They are actively developing attitudes about winning and losing based on what they see and hear.

Meanwhile, parents, if they played sports as kids, have their own positive and negative experiences and attitudes about the same topics, all shaping what they see happening to their offspring. A coach for one of our children’s soccer teams referred to these potentially menacing parental memories as “shark music.”

Sports can be equally joyful, enlivening, challenging, and defeating. There are skills and rules to be learned, and they are not all in rule books. Big emotions are felt and have to be managed, and all bodies must be protected.

Sportsmanship is the ethical environment that keeps the game fair, while all players and officials are respected. The more one loves a sport, the easier it is to get caught up in a “winning-is-everything” mentality. We’ve all seen it: gloating, dissing opponents, yelling at officials, and cheering after a missed free throw. What can we do to help young children like Sam learn to play games in ways that develop positive skills and lead to a lifetime of fun?

  • Help your kids learn the rules. They typically want to know them, having figured out early that if a game is not “fair,” it’s not fun. Rules improve the odds of fairness. The older adults among us come to realize fairness is more aspirational than achievable, but let’s give them a few more years of grace.
  • Listening to coaches and officials is part of building skills. While respect is mostly earned, it helps kids if parents show respectful attitudes toward other adults from the start. This means holding off on the arguing from the sidelines.
  • Everybody plays. That is the epitome of fairness. Leave it to the pros to cut underperformers. It has no place in children’s sports. The "Sams" are very sensitive to this message, even if they are a “better” player.
  • Teach respect for opponents. That means don't brag when winning, accept defeat when losing, and respect the victor’s abilities. One of our son’s teammates, with a streak of an old soul, put it aptly: “Winning is always nice, but it’s really not that big a deal.” Teach and model gracious winning and losing.
  • When someone makes a mistake, let the coach handle it, assuming they will learn something from it, as opposed to being critical or teasing. Personally, I’ve never felt it was reassuring to say to a child, “Well, you did your best.” Neither I nor they know at any given point in their life what their “best” might be (I’m still trying to sort mine out…).
article continues after advertisement

Sports can be a great physical outlet and learning opportunity for young children. The onus is on the adults to make sure that the life-lesson learning experience happens.

item.title: Why Group Fitness Feels So Good
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Why Group Fitness Feels So Good

Moving with others supports connection, confidence, body trust, and belonging.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Group fitness can offer shared rhythm, social reinforcement, and belonging.
  • Shared movement enables co-regulation, signaling safety and easing emotional distress.
  • Inclusive movement spaces help people participate with less self-protection.
Source: Courtesy of Getting Better

On Getting Better With Jonathan Van Ness, I talked about why group fitness can feel so emotionally different from working out alone. The short answer is that movement is more than a physical process; it is a psychological and relational one, too. When we move near other people, we are relating, sensing, responding, and regulating.

Humans are wired for connection. We create community through shared experiences, and movement is one of the most powerful shared experiences we have. Fitness classes, team sports, dance, walking groups, yoga, pickleball leagues, and recreational sports can all become deeply relational because they ask us to be present in our bodies around other people.

That can be energizing, vulnerable, healing, or scary, depending on what our bodies have learned to expect. At its best, group fitness is about expanding our sense of connection, capability, and belonging.

Movement Is Not a Punishment

One of the most common and painful ways people talk about exercise is as punishment.

“I ate dessert, so I have to work out.”

“I went out last night, so I need to make up for it.”

“I don’t like my body, so I need to fix it.”

That mindset turns movement into shame. It frames the body as a problem to solve rather than a body to inhabit, listen to, and care for.

Movement should not be punishment for living our lives. It can be a platform for connection, curiosity, enjoyment, and meaning-making. It can help us release stress, reconnect with ourselves, build confidence, and spend meaningful time with other people.

When movement feels like care instead of correction, people are more likely to return to it. They are also more likely to experience it as something sustainable, not something they simply have to endure.

Movement Is a Mental Health Skill

Physical activity can support mental health in ways that have nothing to do with aesthetics. Research suggests that physical activity interventions can reduce symptoms of depression, anxiety, and psychological distress (Singh et al., 2023).

Movement can help us regulate difficult emotions. It can interrupt anxious thoughts. It can give the mind a break from overthinking. It can also increase flexible thinking and problem-solving when life feels stressful.

There is also something psychologically powerful about doing something hard and realizing, “I can do this.”

Every time someone tries a new movement, stays present through discomfort, modifies when needed, or returns after a difficult day, they build evidence of their own agency. They prove to themselves that they can navigate stress, uncertainty, and challenge.

For people who have experienced trauma, body shame, exclusion, or difficult relationships with their bodies, movement can also help rebuild trust with the body and the self.

Group Movement Gives Us Something Different

Source: Gabin Vallet / Unsplash

Group movement offers something solo exercise sometimes cannot: shared rhythm, social reinforcement, and collective engagement.

Research on group exercise suggests that collective movement and social bonding can reinforce one another, helping explain why group fitness may feel connecting and motivating (Davis et al., 2015).

Think about breathing together in yoga, walking at the same pace with a friend, dancing in a class, rowing in rhythm, or pushing through the final minutes of a workout beside someone else.

Those moments can create a sense of being part of something larger than yourself. You are not just completing a task alone; you are moving with others toward a shared experience.

There is also power in watching other people struggle, pause, laugh, modify, recover, and keep going. It gives permission. It reminds us that effort does not have to look perfect to be meaningful.

Co-Regulation in Motion

Moving in sync with others can support co-regulation by signaling safety to the nervous system.

Co-regulation is the process of feeling steadier through connection with another person or group. In movement spaces, this can happen through shared breath, rhythm, eye contact, encouragement, music, laughter, and the simple awareness that other people are doing hard things too.

A group class can help someone feel less alone in their effort. A team can give someone a sense of mutual commitment. A recreational league can offer play, structure, and belonging that might be lacking elsewhere in someone’s life.

These experiences can improve mood, deepen connection, and help people access the body’s rest-and-recovery systems after stress.

Inclusive Movement Spaces

Source: Unsplash

Most fitness and sport spaces were not designed with everyone in mind.

Race, gender, queerness, body size, disability, class, and lived experience all shape access, safety, visibility, and belonging. If someone has experienced support, affirmation, and belonging in fitness environments, group movement may feel motivating. But if someone has experienced judgment, exclusion, racism, anti-fat bias, ableism, homophobia, transphobia, or public embarrassment, that same environment may feel threatening.

A sign that says “all are welcome” is not enough. Inclusion has to be built into the walls of fitness and sport spaces, and lived through the daily offerings, practices, and environments those spaces create.

It has to show up in the language instructors use. It has to show up in who is hired, represented, and protected. It has to show up in pricing, accessibility, modifications, music, policies, changing spaces, leadership, and clear responses when harm occurs.

Real inclusion is not reflected in how a space describes itself; it is reflected in how people actually experience that space every day.

For LGBTQ+ people and other minoritized communities, affirming movement spaces can reduce the burden of identity-related stress. When people do not have to constantly monitor, protect, explain, or edit themselves, they often have more capacity for movement, enjoyment, connection, and performance.

Inclusive spaces make it possible for people to participate more fully once they arrive.

What a Movement Community Can Change

Source: Sherise Van Dyk / Pexels

At its best, a great movement community can change (or even save) someone’s life.

It can transform a person’s sense of belonging. It can bring people out of loneliness. It can improve their relationship with themselves, with others, and with their bodies. It can offer a healthier way to cope with stress, grief, recovery, anxiety, or disconnection.

It can give adults permission to play.

It can give queer athletes and performers space to move as their full selves. It can give people across identities a shared court, class, team, or rhythm. It can help someone find not just an exercise routine, but a reason to keep coming back.

Movement is powerful on its own.

Movement with others can be transformative.

item.title: Therapists with Paws Help Ukrainians with PTSD
item.description:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder

Therapists with Paws Help Ukrainians with PTSD

In Ukraine, dogs help traumatized individuals feel safe again.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • At a Ukrainian K9 center in Ukraine, dogs are helping POWs recover from trauma.
  • Therapy dogs support grounding, co-regulation, graded exposure, and behavioral activation.
  • The dogs are chosen for different jobs according to their temperaments.

At a Ukrainian police canine facility about a 40-minute drive from Kyiv, dogs are being used to do something trauma survivors often struggle with: Persuade the nervous system that danger has ended.

Some of the people treated there are former prisoners of war whom Russian captors tormented with attack dogs. For them, even an ordinary village dog can become a danger cue. The animal may be harmless, but the nervous system does not know that yet. A glimpse of teeth, a sudden bark, or a dog moving too quickly can trigger panic, flashbacks, or the frozen terror of captivity. After repeated exposure to dogs trained to menace, bite, or intimidate, the brain can form an intense conditioned fear response: Dog means danger.

At the Cynological Center of the Main Department of the National Police in Kyiv Region,shortened here to the K9 Center, the premise is that a brain that has learned fear can, under the right conditions, unlearn that fear

The word cynological means the study of dogs. Svitlana Kolomiets, head of the Unit for the Organization of Canine Activities of the National Police of Ukraine, describes the dogs there as full members of police work. “A dog can be just as much a part of the police force as an officer,” she said.

At the K9 Center, that statement is not metaphorical. Dogs search for explosives, pursue suspects, detect narcotics, locate missing people, and help people with PTSD symptoms begin to tolerate what once terrified them.

Exposure Therapy with a Tail

For former prisoners of war whom the Russians terrorized with vicious dogs, treatment may begin with a chihuahua. A person who can’t endure being near a large dog often can manage well enough with a tiny, nonthreatening one. Gradually, when the former POW has become comfortable with the chihuahua, he or she will be introduced to a slightly larger dog, perhaps a terrier-size dog. Eventually, the person may be brought near a full-size Belgian Malinois, the same breed that the Russians used to bite the prisoner, leaving him or her helpless and in pain.

The therapists use such systematic desensitization to enable the patient to unlearn the old association that says, “Dog equals life-threatening danger.” Bit by bit, the new association is, “Dogs don’t mean danger.”

The Leaning Dogs

Belgian Malinois Therapy Dog "leans" against soldier
Source: Svitlana Kolomiets, used with permission

Another approach to recovery from PTSD symptoms is the use of emotional-support dogs trained to lean against people. A friendly Belgian Malinois may walk up to a visitor, tail wagging, exuding friendliness, and in something unexpected for normal dog behavior, press its warm, furry body against the visitor’s leg. This surprising behavior has been carefully trained.

article continues after advertisement

The therapy dogs learn to do this with patients who may be frightened, withdrawn, or experiencing PTSD symptoms. A traumatized person may resist the touch of another human being even though it’s known that touch can help a person with PTSD feel better. In the experience of the therapists at the K9 Center, a person who resists human touch may quickly get comfortable with a gentle dog that’s wagging its tail, pressing against them, and giving every sign of enjoying being near the person.

The dog’s leaning behavior helps provide somatic grounding; that is, the patient starts paying attention to his or her body in the present moment. At its best, the leaning behavior supports co-regulation, the process by which the dog’s own calm nervous system helps calm the patient’s nervous system.

HR for Dogs

Dogs begin being tracked for different roles at two months of age. The center staff notice the animal’s personality. A friendly, steady puppy that is happy around people may become a therapy dog. A calm, focused dog may be trained for detecting explosives or narcotics in crowded places.

A highly aggressive dog may receive training for chasing and detaining vicious criminals. As one therapist joked, “These dogs are the psychopaths,” and another referred to them as “the Beasts.” However, such monikers are not a staff tradition. Rather, the dogs are viewed as uniquely qualified by temperament for their important work.

Rehabilitation Disguised as Kindness

Visitors to the K9 Center get to see some rehabilitation exercises that, at first glance, look charmingly ridiculous. However, there’s a psychological rationale.

A wounded person relearning motor control may be asked to use chopsticks to pick up morsels of food to feed a dog. The exercise requires attention, coordination, emotional control, and patience. It is sensorimotor rehabilitation disguised as kindness.

article continues after advertisement

For someone depressed or withdrawn, it can also become behavioral activation: a small, rewarding action that pulls the person back into engagement. The dog receives the food and rewards the patient with attention and tail wags.

A depressed person may resist cooperating with a human therapist but will engage in the exercise when there’s a dog in front of him or her, alert and eagerly awaiting the next treat.

In Russia’s War on Ukraine, PTSD symptoms are common. At the K9 Center, an approach that works is to give the individual enduring the distress new experiences. They involve four paws, clear commands, controlled danger, and, sometimes, a warm dog leaning against a leg. The process has surprisingly positive results. Over time, people begin to feel and understand an important and healing new thought: I’m safe now.

item.title: What Makes or Breaks a Stepmother-Stepdaughter Relationship
item.description:
Family Dynamics

What Makes or Breaks a Stepmother-Stepdaughter Relationship

What stepmothers and fathers should know before blending their family.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • The stepmother-stepdaughter relationship is often a complicated one, even if rarely discussed openly.
  • A stepmother should confront her insecurities and jealousy, while bringing consistency and patience.
  • A father needs to hold space for both his marriage and the inclusion and connection with his children.

I listened as my client shared an indelible childhood memory. She was 11 years old, watching a movie on the couch with her dad. Enter her new stepmother, Jan, who insisted she move to the end of the couch so Jan could sit next to her dad. Decades later, my client still felt the sting from the way Jan’s insecurities severed the relationship with her father.

Beyond my clients, I’ve heard stories from friends as well. One friend, now in her 50s, said her stepmother, Sue, still holds it against her that she was prickly upon meeting Sue at age 13, despite it being typical (and understandable) pre-teen behavior.

Why are so many stepmother-stepdaughter relationships fraught with problems?

Few relationships in families carry as much unspoken weight as the one between a stepmother and a stepdaughter. Unlike most bonds, it’s not chosen; it’s inherited—often under challenging circumstances. It begins in the aftermath of loss: loss through divorce, death, or the fracturing of a family that a child (youth or adult) never wanted fractured. And into that tender space, a new woman arrives.

Sometimes the relationship blooms into something lovely. But often—more often than we talk about openly—it becomes a source of lasting pain. Not because blended families are inherently broken, but because the adults in them sometimes fail to rise to the emotional demands the situation requires.

The Unique Tensions of This Bond

The stepmother-stepdaughter relationship is unlike almost any other. A stepdaughter, whether she is 7 or 37, arrives with a loyalty already spoken for. She loves her father. She may still grieve for her original family. She didn’t ask for a new woman to enter her father's life, and she certainly didn't ask to be expected to welcome her unconditionally.

The stepmother, for her own part, may have entered the relationship with genuine warmth and good intentions—only to find herself tested or quietly resented. Or she may have come in with her own insecurities, unresolved wounds, and an unconscious need for control.

What makes the dynamic so combustible is that both parties are frequently reacting to fears they can’t fully name.

When a Stepmother's Insecurity Becomes a Child's Wound

One of the most damaging—and least discussed—patterns in stepfamily life is stepmother jealousy. Not jealousy of a romantic rival, but jealousy of a child. Of a daughter's claim on her father's love, time, history, and attention.

It can manifest in subtle ways: a stepmother who quietly undermines a stepdaughter's confidence, who competes for the father's approval, who reframes the daughter's needs as manipulation or drama, who creates friction around visits, holidays, or milestones. It can also be far less subtle—outright hostility, exclusion, or a systematic campaign to reposition herself as the center of the family at the expense of the children.

What makes this pattern so harmful is that children—including adult children—are rarely in a position to name it for what it is. They feel the rejection, the coldness, the sense that they are somehow "too much" or "in the way," but they internalize it as a reflection of their own worth rather than a reflection of the stepmother's unresolved fears and insecurities.

The damage rarely stays contained to the stepmother relationship. Family rejection and emotional insecurity can ripple outward—affecting self-esteem, attachment patterns in future relationships, and even the child's relationship with their biological father, who is often caught in the middle.

The Father's Responsibility

And that brings us to the figure who is almost always at the center of the story: the father. A father who remarries does not stop being a father. His children did not stop being his children, no matter their age. Yet one of the most painful realities stepdaughters describe is the experience of watching their father disappear—not physically, but emotionally—as he prioritizes his new marriage, and perhaps new stepchildren, over his existing relationships with his kids.

This is often the path of least resistance. Keeping the peace at home is easier than confronting a spouse's unreasonable behavior. Avoiding conflict feels like protecting the marriage. But what it actually does is send a devastating message to the child: You are negotiable. She is not.

A mature father understands that loving his wife and protecting his children are not competing obligations. He doesn’t ask his daughter to manage his wife's emotions. He doesn’t punish his daughter for failing to bond on command. He sets clear expectations within his marriage about how his children are to be treated—and he holds to them, even when it’s uncomfortable.

What Maturity Actually Looks Like

Neither the stepmother nor the father gets to opt out of the emotional work that blended family life requires. For a stepmother, maturity means being honest with herself about her own insecurities rather than acting them out on a child. It means accepting that her stepdaughter's love for her father is not a threat to her marriage. It means understanding that she does not need to replace the child's mother, nor compete with her. Her role is not to be loved unconditionally from day one—it is to be safe, fair, and consistent, and to let trust grow on the child's timeline, not her own.

For a father, maturity means holding two truths at once: that his marriage matters, and that his children matter. It means being willing to have hard conversations with his partner about behavior that harms his kids. And it means never, ever making his child feel that his love for her is contingent on her relationship with his wife.

When the Child Is Already an Adult

A common misconception is that these dynamics only affect young children. In reality, adult stepdaughters often describe some of the sharpest pain—precisely because they are expected to "handle it."

An adult daughter who watches her father remarry may find herself suddenly on the outside of family gatherings, excluded from decisions, or quietly written out of a family narrative she spent decades helping to build. The stepmother who resents her may do so with a sophistication that is hard to name.

And the father who is supposed to be a peer to his adult daughter—someone she can speak to honestly—may instead become unavailable, defensive, or parroting his wife's framing of events.

The wound is no less real for being inflicted on a grown woman. If anything, it’s more disorienting because she is old enough to understand exactly what is happening but still powerless to change it.

Not all stepmother-stepdaughter stories end in estrangement or tension. Many blended families do find their footing—not because everyone pretended the complexity wasn't there but because the adults in the room chose accountability.

The stepmothers who are remembered with warmth are the ones who showed up with respect, patience, and an absence of an agenda. The fathers who maintained strong relationships with their daughters through a remarriage were the ones who never made their daughters choose.

Blended families can come with their challenges. They require more emotional generosity, more honest communication, and more willingness to sit with discomfort than most nuclear families ever face. But the children in them—whether young or grown—deserve adults who rise to the occasion. They didn't ask to be in a blended family. The least the adults can do is make it a safe one.

item.title: How Eating Disorders Convince People to Delay Recovery
item.description:
Eating Disorders

How Eating Disorders Convince People to Delay Recovery

The illness creates a feeling that postponing recovery is "practical."

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Recovery from an eating disorder can begin even when ambivalence and fear are still present.
  • Eating disorders tend to become more disruptive when left untreated over time.
  • Progress in eating disorder recovery often starts before a patient is fully certain about the process.
Source: Photo by Katie Moum on Unsplash

Many people imagine eating disorder recovery as something they will begin once they feel fully ready, after the semester ends, work calms down, or life becomes less complicated. They often believe there will eventually be a better time to address the eating disorder, one that feels less disruptive, less emotionally overwhelming, or less inconvenient.

But eating disorders rarely work that way because the illness itself often convinces people that delaying recovery is responsible, practical, or temporary. At the same time, part of the disorder may still feel comforting, protective, or difficult to let go of, leading people to believe they can hold onto parts of it while still moving toward health. This is one of the hardest realities about eating disorders: The illness often shapes the belief that now is not the right time to recover.

“I’m Not Ready Yet”

Many people think they need to feel completely motivated before starting treatment, but readiness is often misunderstood. You do not have to want recovery more than the eating disorder before you begin, because many people enter treatment feeling scared, uncertain, resistant, or deeply ambivalent. They may fear weight changes, emotional overwhelm, loss of control, or giving up something that has helped them cope.

That ambivalence is not a sign to wait, because it is often part of the illness itself. If people only pursued recovery once they felt completely ready, many would never begin, and many people who eventually recover look back and realize they started long before they felt fully certain.

The Illusion of “Waiting Until Later”

A common belief is that the eating disorder can be managed until life slows down. Students may avoid higher levels of care to avoid disrupting school; professionals may fear stepping away from work; athletes may worry about losing momentum; and parents may feel guilty about prioritizing treatment.

But eating disorders are progressive illnesses that tend to become more consuming over time, not less. What many people do not recognize is that delaying treatment often creates far greater disruption later. I have seen people try to push through until their body or mind could no longer sustain it, resulting in emergency medical issues, psychiatric hospitalization, academic withdrawal, damaged relationships, or years of life overtaken by the disorder.

The interruption they feared eventually happened anyway, often in a far more painful way than if treatment had been pursued earlier. Many people postpone recovery because they are trying to preserve their current life, but untreated eating disorders often shrink life over time, physically, emotionally, socially, and cognitively.

Recovery Does Not Require Certainty

You do not need complete confidence to take the next step, stop being afraid, or know exactly who you are without the eating disorder before beginning treatment. Sometimes recovery starts with something much smaller, such as allowing the possibility that waiting may not actually protect your future in the way the disorder promises it will.

There may never be a perfectly convenient moment to seek help. Recovery rarely begins with certainty. More often, it begins with a willingness to question what the eating disorder has told you about safety, control, and what is possible for your life.

If treatment feels disruptive, it is worth asking what the eating disorder is already disrupting. Your health, relationships, opportunities, and peace of mind matter. Your life is worth making room for, and worth getting help for, even before you feel completely ready.

item.title: Why We Follow Leaders, and When and Why We Don’t
item.description:
Leadership

Why We Follow Leaders, and When and Why We Don’t

Why some follow leaders blindly, and what causes people to resist.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • People’s tendency to follow leaders is a “default” system of submissiveness.
  • Psychological processes, including conformity and obedience to authority, are reasons why people follow.
  • Deciding not to follow often involves calculation of costs and benefits for not following.

Since the dawn of human existence, there have been leaders and followers. There is voluminous research and writing about leaders and leadership. There is much less written about followers and following. We know why leaders lead—they get status and benefits, and they can move others toward goals (their personal goals or shared goals). But why do followers follow, and importantly, when do they choose to not follow established leaders?

This is the topic of leadership scholar Barbara Kellerman’s new book, Why We Follow Leaders, and Why We Don’t. The book is one of the most detailed analyses of followership and the reasons for following (or not following).

Why We Follow Leaders

Kellerman begins with the premise that humans, like so many species of social animals, are “programmed” to follow—to be submissive. She also asserts that human civilization has built hierarchies and that those in subordinate positions typically default to the followership role. Drawing on both ethological and psychological theories, we tend to follow because it is in our best interests (we are rewarded, or not punished, for following—think obedience to authority and Milgram’s work). We also follow because others are following (conformity), or simply because of our tendency to go along, as the path of least resistance.

Obviously, as Kellerman notes in separate chapters, there are rewards given to willing followers and punishments for those who refuse to follow. Loyal followers often benefit from obediently following the leader, and followers who are reluctant or refuse to follow can be threatened and punished. Kellerman draws on numerous examples from work organizations, politics, and social movements.

Why Might We Refuse to Follow Leaders?

Perhaps the biggest contributions to our understanding of leadership and followership comes from Kellerman’s analysis of why normally submissive followers might refuse to follow a leader. In some instances, think of revolutions or workers going on strike, there are potential rewards (attainment of leadership positions, pay increases, respectively) for not following.

There may also be punishments as a result of following a leader—particularly a “bad” leader, as suggested by Hitler’s underlings who were held responsible, convicted, and sometimes executed because they argued that they were “simply following orders.” The example of the mass suicide/murder of the followers of the Reverend Jim Jones in Jonestown is a perfect example of how willingly following can lead to disaster.

In all of the discussion of followership, Kellerman emphasizes the importance of situational factors in whether followers choose to follow or resist. For example, if a leader falls out of favor due to bad behavior or leadership failures, followers may be reluctant to follow.

Given the fact that we are all followers at some level (Kellerman points out that as voters we are, by definition, followers of elected leaders, and most employees follow a supervisor/leader), understanding why and when we follow, and why we might choose to resist, is critically important. The negative stereotype of followers as “blind sheep” is only partially true, as there is a human tendency to go along and not “make waves.” There are, however, many instances where followers decide not to follow and may use their influence to resist. And, in the case of destructive and toxic leaders, it is imperative that followers resist, as it is the only way to bring down tyrants. I can also recommend Ira Chaleff’s recent book, To Stop a Tyrant.

item.title: The Rise of the Beta Mom
item.description:
Parenting

The Rise of the Beta Mom

Are "beta moms" a new trend, or just a return to reasonable parenting?

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • "Beta moms" embrace relaxed parenting, rejecting over-scheduled, intensive child management.
  • The beta mom trend echoes past authoritative parenting, balancing support and independence.
  • Parents benefit mentally by releasing the pressure of invisible labor and unattainable perfection.
Source: Michael Sauers/Flickr

Last month, the Wall Street Journal published an article entitled “The Era of the Tiger Mom Is Over. Enter the Beta Mom.” It refers to a recent TikTok trend featuring moms who reject intensive, highly managed parenting in favor of a more relaxed approach.

A Pushback Against Helicopter Parenting

The “beta moms” are pushing back against a trend that started in the early 1990s favoring hyper-involved parenting, especially for mothers, stemming from a growing knowledge-based economy that made a lot of parents fear that their children would fall behind their peers if they didn’t have a competitive edge. What we ended up with was a lot of helicopter parents, who are overly involved in their children’s lives, especially in academic or achievement-related activities (Odenweller et al., 2014).

A helicopter parent removes obstacles that their children face in order to encourage them to succeed. These parents are generally well-educated, well-resourced, and very well-intentioned—mostly just trying to protect their kids from trouble and provide them with opportunities.

But despite the good intentions of most over-involved parents, children of helicopter parents don’t necessarily perform well in school. In fact, helicopter parenting is associated with lower academic performance in children, more extrinsic or reward-based motivation, and avoidance goals for learning (Schiffrin & Liss, 2017). Further, according to a recent meta-analysis of over 200 studies, helicopter parenting is associated with increased anxiety symptoms in children (Ryan et al., 2026).

A Rejection of Invisible Labor in Favor of "Good Enough" Parenting

The “beta mom” trend also seems to be a direct result of mothers being overwhelmed by the invisible labor involved in being a parent, and are rejecting the over-planning, over-scheduling, and over-management of their children. These parents are opting for less structured schedules, more independence for their children, and the idea that accepting the mess and imperfection of a less hands-on approach is “good enough” parenting.

This approach seems completely logical. But is it really all that new?

Back in the 1960s, Diana Baumrind from the University of California at Berkeley famously identified several distinct parenting styles. The “authoritarian” parents she observed 60 years ago were a lot like the helicopter parents of today: They had very high standards for their children’s behavior and exerted a large amount of control, allowing children very little autonomy. In contrast, the “authoritative” parents were supportive, had reasonable expectations about their children’s behavior, but were less hands-on than the authoritarian parents. And perhaps most importantly, authoritative parents were flexible—they got more relaxed about rules as their children matured, which resulted in children who could also flexibly deal with the challenges they faced (Baumrind, 1966). In fact, Baumrind found that children of authoritative parents were the most well-adjusted, and the most likely to be independent and well-socialized.

article continues after advertisement

This work happened around the same time that British pediatrician and psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott coined the term “good enough mother” when he noticed that children benefit from watching parents make mistakes. He argued that kids develop better coping skills when their parents are reliable and responsive to their needs, but not necessarily perfect. By denying children a model for making mistakes, parents deny them the ability to develop the flexibility to learn from those mistakes and bounce back from them (LeMoyne & Buchanan, 2011). In fact, cognitive flexibility is one of the best predictors of academic achievement (e.g., Blair & Raver, 2014).

So although the idea of the “beta-mom” might not necessarily be new, it is definitely a step in the right direction—a step towards returning to reasonable parenting expectations. As a parent, I know very well that we all want to put our kids first, but that doesn’t mean completely abandoning our own needs, and it certainly doesn’t mean doing everything for our children. Making mistakes in front of them isn’t a bad thing; it normalizes mistake-making and models how to recover from those mistakes. In the end, there is no perfect parenting, and sometimes being “good enough” is actually what’s best for our kids.

item.title: How to Biohack Your Brain
item.description:
Health

How to Biohack Your Brain

Biohacking may just be a combo of ancient practices and new technologies.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows oxygen, cellular energy, and electromagnetic therapies strengthen the body's repair systems.
  • Our studies and others show that ancient practices like meditation and breathwork are biohacking, too.
  • The future of healing may be a combination of both new and ancient modalities.

A few years ago, I had a health crisis that had me lying down and unable to really function. I had extreme chronic fatigue, low energy, and even felt like my memory and cognition were not what they once were. A doctor offered medication to mask my symptoms. I declined—not out of contrarianism, but because I understood enough about physiology to know that suppressing signals rarely addresses their source. I was worried I'd burn my body out further by masking symptoms and have to pay a steeper price later.

That's when, through a friend, I discovered hyperbaric oxygen chamber therapy. I was really surprised to find out that not only did my energy come back, but so did my ability to be creative. In fact, I wrote my second book, SOVEREIGN, in six months.

Alongside the hyperbaric sessions, I was also using IV therapies like NAD+ and Niagen, compounds said to support cellular energy production and brain function. Together, these two approaches—experimental as they felt at the time—seemed to be giving my body the raw materials it needed to repair itself. Or was it all placebo?

Evaluating the Science Behind Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy

As a research scientist, I needed to understand this better. I found that by delivering concentrated oxygen to the brain and reducing neuroinflammation, hyperbaric oxygen therapy has been shown to improve cognition, memory, and focus. A 2024 review in Frontiers in Neurology described it as an emerging neuromodulatory technique with applications across a range of neurological conditions, and a systematic review in Neuropsychological Review found positive effects on cognitive function across multiple patient populations. At the hyperbaric center I went to for my sessions, I met stroke patients who swore the chamber had given them their life back, veterans with traumatic brain injury and anxiety, parents of kids with autism, and older adults with dementia. Could something as simple as oxygen help all of these people? The science is still developing, but the underlying idea is compelling: Rather than treating disease after it arrives, what if we could strengthen the body's own systems?

Biohacking is a term that was first coined by Dave Asprey, a Silicon Valley entrepreneur intent on finding the key to longevity and optimal human health. That's when I realized I had been doing a version of it for years without calling it that. I'd spent my career at Stanford and Yale researching holistic and functional ways we can improve our mental health through what we could perhaps call "ancient biohacking."

The research we conducted has looked at loving-kindness meditation and its impact on well-being, social connection, and chronic pain. We have seen how breathing techniques like Sky Breath Meditation can heal posttraumatic stress in veterans returning from war and help stressed college students cultivate resilience and prevent mental health crises. We've also examined how relationships and social connection can improve the rate of healing, increase physical health, and even extend longevity. And we've seen how exercising compassion can fight off burnout, erase the impact of stress on longevity, and reduce inflammation at the cellular level. Traditional and ancient methodologies, it turns out, are powerful technologies in their own right.

My personal experience with HBOT and IV therapy opened my eyes to what newer technologies might also offer. Pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy, for instance, is showing real promise: a 2024 study in Scientific Reports found that PEMF accelerated the formation of new blood vessels by shifting how cells produce and use energy at the mitochondrial level, and a 2025 systematic review found meaningful benefits for pain and physical function in patients with chronic low back pain. The thread connecting all of these approaches—oxygen, cellular energy, electromagnetic stimulation—is that they work with the body's existing repair systems rather than overriding them.

That curiosity eventually led me to Dave Asprey's biohacking conference, where I experienced this world firsthand—breathing in hydrogen, placing my body in various devices, and encountering everything from frequency and electricity to red, blue, and green light therapies.

The conference floor also included technologies I could not evaluate: devices combining multiple modalities simultaneously, frequency-based interventions, and approaches that are either decades ahead of the published research or waiting to be tested by it. I wanted to try one of the many "med beds" combining red light, sound frequency, and ozone therapy in a single session, but people lined up at 7 a.m. to get on the list. I did spend some time in a large copper geometric enclosure emitting what were described as coherent frequencies, and found it genuinely relaxing—though there's obviously a gap between subjective experience and controlled evidence. I tried a meditation device that sent my companion into deep parasympathetic rest and had me agitated.

Combining Ancient and Modern Modalities

As a scientist who has spent my career studying mental health, well-being, and resilience, I am excited about the future of healing (and the possibilities of further biohacking our brains!) when we combine ancient technologies like meditation, breathwork, and yoga with newer ones designed to strengthen the body's ability to heal and detoxify itself. When I asked Dave Asprey about the future of biohacking, he said: personalization.

And that's interesting, too. We are all different, with different bodies, different needs, and different histories. It makes sense that we would benefit from different modalities, at different doses, in different combinations. The fascinating question is how we figure that out at scale—and that may be where artificial intelligence comes in.

item.title: Complementary Work-Life Balance in Marriage
item.description:
Marriage

Complementary Work-Life Balance in Marriage

How happy couples blend personal and professional life.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Men and women have different criteria for marital satisfaction.
  • Many couples report successful marriages despite working demanding jobs.
  • With proactivity and patience, both traditional and modern couples can blend work and family.

In modern society, many couples do not have the luxury of having one spouse stay home to raise children while the other provides complete financial support. Instead, they struggle to make ends meet in a difficult economy where both parents are working. Raising a family within a dual-income marriage requires motivation, money, and multitasking. Fortunately, however, many couples are able to make it work. Positive work-life blend fuels happy, satisfying marriages and productive work schedules for both husbands and wives. Research explains.

Source: Alisa Dyson / Pixabay

Dual-Income Marital Work-Life Blend

Kaarina Määttä and Satu Uusiautti (2012) investigated factors contributing to the ability to balance work and family within marriage through soliciting input from hundreds of couples who have been married for more than a decade and have been able to combine family life with demanding work schedules.[i] Most of the participants had been married between 10 and 15 years, had one or two children, and worked either outside the home or from home—excluding domestic work, which was not considered “work” for purposes of the study.

Participants discussed the relational elements that contributed to marital stability and happiness, yielding seven “rules of personal behavior” leading to a satisfying marriage and work-life blend. Määttä and Uusiautti found that none of the couples in their study had avoided challenges. Instead, they developed “personal models of interaction” leading to the proverbial secret of marital success.

Work-Life Blend Works Both Ways

Regarding the interaction between work and family, Määttä and Uusiautti note that it is a two-way street with a border that is flexible and able to blend. While they note that the work-family life connection has been examined predominantly from a negative conflict perspective, they acknowledge that this interplay also has positive consequences, sharing some common features.

Their study identified seven rules for enjoying a happy marriage while also working:

  • The ability to turn the downs into ups
  • Activity, creativity, and imagination
  • Tolerating the dissimilarity and change
  • Patience, flexibility, and humbleness
  • Acknowledging, supporting, and admiring
  • Commitment and dedication
  • Respecting oneself

Gender Role Expectations

Many partners may identify with this list as productive ways to navigate any relationship, romantic or otherwise. Yet within marriages, there is more to the equation. In addition to these seven rules, as a practical matter, there are gender differences in successful work-life blended marriages. Määttä and Uusiautti cite prior research (Pedersen Stevens, Minnotte, Mannon, & Kiger, 2007) for the proposition that in dual-income relationships, men view relationship satisfaction as linked with “positive family-to-work spillover,” and for women, positive spillover is tied to satisfaction with the housework arrangement. Because, as Määttä and Uusiautti recognize, men and women are engaging in more nontraditional gender roles both at work and at home, it is more important than ever to understand how these roles impact each partner.

Proactive Marital Positive Planning

To capitalize on the potential for work-life blend, couples should consider differences in gender role expectations when making decisions on family responsibilities. Good communication here is key, particularly within modern marriages where spouses may not subscribe to traditional gender roles in terms of the division of labor. With husbands taking paternity leave and mothers working several jobs (at least temporarily) to acquire health insurance to take care of a young family, good spousal communication ensures role expectations and housework responsibilities are clear and agreeable to both partners. A happy home fuels a productive workday, and the spouse in the workforce knows what is expected upon arriving back at the haven of home base.

With proactivity and patience, both traditional and modern couples can enjoy both health and wealth, family and financial stability, love and marital longevity, till death do they part.
