item.title: How to Survive the Sting of Artistic Criticism
item.description:
Resilience

How to Survive the Sting of Artistic Criticism

How artists can navigate negative public feedback without losing self-worth.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • The brain remembers cruelty more vividly than praise, which is why bad reviews linger.
  • A critic judges in one evening what an artist built over weeks of rehearsal and self-revelation.
  • A review reflects one person's taste on one night, not a verdict on an artist's worth or future.
  • Shame thrives in silence; spoken aloud to someone who's been there, a bad review loses its grip.

"Places, please!"

Rosalie stands alone in her dressing room, listening to the murmur of the audience beyond the walls. She takes a steadying breath, smooths her costume, then nods at her reflection, as if borrowing courage from the woman looking back.

She is 23, fresh from her MFA, and about to open her first leading role at a renowned repertory theatre.

Beneath her focus runs a quieter current, an anxiety so many performers carry in secret: What if I'm not enough? What if I don't belong?

When the curtain rises, she gives everything she has.

The night ends in uproarious applause. Flowers crowd her dressing room, tucked with notes from agents, family, and friends. She feels pride and disbelief, the fragile astonishment of a dream becoming real. Years of longing and sacrifice have culminated in this glittering moment.

The next morning, the reviews are published.

They are blunt. Cutting. Forever attached to her name.

Rosalie reads them in bed before her feet touch the floor. By day's end, she can recite the cruelest sentences more fluently than her own lines. As the season continues, she performs beneath the weight of perceived public failure. The openness she first carried onto the stage collapses under self-consciousness and dread.

An actress reads a negative review.
Source: Pheelings Media / iStock

When Critique Becomes a Verdict

For performers, the personal and professional are inseparable. Their voice, body, instinct, and imagination are the instruments of their trade. When a critic dismisses a performance, their words may land as an attack on the self. Psychologists call this ego threat: feedback that strikes at who we are, rather than what we have done.

Ask any performer, and they can quote their worst review word for word, decades later. Almost no one can quote their best. Why?

Negativity bias. The brain registers negative information more powerfully than positive. An ancestor who flinched at the rustle in the grass was more likely to survive than one who remained cheerfully oblivious. Having once kept us alive, this survival instinct can now magnify a single criticism until it overshadows a season of standing ovations.

Contingent self-worth. Fine-tuning their craft through applause, laughter, and director's notes, artists learn early to anchor their value in external approval. With self-worth hinging on factors outside their control, every review can become a referendum on their right to belong. In a career defined by scarcity and instability, a single bad review can feel like a death knell for a precarious livelihood.

Rumination. Each rereading tells Rosalie's nervous system the threat is happening now. Social-evaluative threat activates the same stress circuitry as physical danger, shifting the brain into protective mode. We close down. We stop listening, stop creating, stop taking risks. Creativity requires openness. Threat demands self-protection. The two cannot share the stage.

Then there is the cruelty of permanence. Reviews once lined hamster cages by the weekend; now they are indexed and shared by algorithms. Yet the proven spotlight effect offers some comfort: We overestimate how much others notice and remember our imperfections. Audiences move on far faster than we think, and are more forgiving, and more forgetful, of a scathing critique than the artist who carries it.

Taking Back the Narrative

There are ways to soften the blow without abandoning the reasons you walked onstage in the first place. Performing, at its best, is an act of courage and generosity. We brave the spotlight so that strangers in the dark might recognize something of their own humanity in our work. The strategies that follow may help you protect what matters most: the work itself, and the part of you brave enough to keep making it.

  • Decide how you'll engage before opening night. Reading reviews is a choice, not an obligation. Many performers never do; others wait until the run has closed. Harsh words lodge in memory, resurfacing at the worst possible moments: mid-scene, mid-line, mid-song. Protect your peace by setting boundaries in advance.
  • Remember who did the work. A review evaluates one performance, on one night, filtered through one person's taste, history, and mood. Their response is shaped by their expectations and preexisting attitudes toward the genre, playwright, or company. Whatever they conclude, remember this: They did not do the creative work—the searching, collaboration, and laying bare of the self that brings a story to life. A review can be dashed off in a hotel room over a nightcap. You gave it your heart across weeks of rehearsal. Honour that.
  • Say it out loud. Shame survives by convincing us we are uniquely defective and must keep quiet. Tell a trusted castmate, "That review gutted me," and notice how quickly "me too" comes back. Ask seasoned actors about their reviews. Google your favourite Broadway or Hollywood actors and read about theirs. You will be hard-pressed to find an artist who has not suffered bad press.
  • Trade the worst ones. Have a bad-review-off. Find the comedy in the cruelty and the absurdity in this strange corner of the profession. A scathing review does not exile you; it places you in a lineage of brave artists who were critiqued and carried on.

The Reviews Are Not the Final Word

Rosalie's story did not end with the morning papers. When she confided in an actress she admired, she discovered she was in good company. Then she turned back to what was still hers: the character, the story, the creative work.

She began to hold the review as a passing opinion, not a verdict on her value or a prophecy of her professional future. The critics' voices grew quieter. Before long, playfulness and awe returned.

Somewhere tonight, a performer stands in the wings with a critic's words still ringing in their ears. Still, they walk into the light.

Critics will have their say. But they do not get the final word. That belongs to the artists: the brave hearts who risk, reveal, and return, night after night.

Bravo.

item.title: Autistic Children Are Not Lab Rats
item.description:
Autism

Autistic Children Are Not Lab Rats

Personal Perspective: Untested treatments put autistic kids at risk without proven benefits.

Posted June 15, 2026

Another news article about expensive, experimental autism treatments showed up in my feed this weekend—this time in the British paper, The Guardian.

Over the years, I have read dozens of stories like it. Different families, different “miracle cures,” different groups of professionals or pseudo-professionals pushing it, but essentially the same. Each time, some individual, group, or company is pushing an untested intervention that will cure autism. They prey on desperate families who have insufficient supports for their high-needs children, teens, or adults, who are willing to do anything—and pay any price—to help their loved one.

I have seen individuals push all sorts of cures, such as hyperbaric chambers, expensive chiropractic interventions, bleach water, and even açaí berry juice. Some of these interventions are harmless, some potentially deadly. Some are relatively inexpensive, some cost tens of thousands of dollars—but they all share the common theme of claiming to help cure autism. Then, when it has played out, they move on to some other scheme.

Relaxed Protocols Have Enabled Experimental Autism Treatments

This time around, Robert Kennedy Jr., the United States Secretary of Health and Human Services, has relaxed scientific protocols and standards, allowing for experimental treatments to be administered legally in the U.S. The latest “miracle cures” are stem-cell treatments, given to autistic children, many of whom are nonspeaking, and some as young as 18 months old. Children are restrained or given sedatives, and then the stem cells are injected into their bodies with the promise that it will help improve language and social skills, and reduce problem behaviors. The promised effects are more likely, families are told, if they do repeat treatments, so some cash out their retirement savings or take on second mortgages to afford them.

Is this a good investment? Are stem cells a safe and effective treatment? We don’t really know because this treatment has not been fully researched. But since RFK Jr. has given his blessing and relaxed protocols, we are seeing scientific trials administered in real time, on real people, who may or may not be able to communicate how they feel or give any kind of informed consent.

Exploitation of Vulnerable Populations in Medicine Is Not New

Kennedy may be taking us back more than five decades to the Willowbrook State School era, where disabled children were purposefully given hepatitis A and B from 1956 to 1972. Those children were used as human subjects to allow scientists to study how hepatitis progressed in the human body, and then develop effective vaccines. One of the goals of these current stem-cell trials seems to be to study how they may be used to treat other conditions. So let’s call this out for what it is: state-sanctioned medical testing on vulnerable, disabled populations for the potential eventual benefit of others.

This is exactly the kind of thing that other autistic advocates and I feared when RFK Jr. promised in April 2025 to find a “cure” for autism. In that speech, autism was depicted as something preventable that “destroys families.” Autistic people were described as individuals who would not be able to do things like date, play baseball, write poetry, use the toilet, hold a job, pay taxes, etc. Instead of sharing some of the most challenging aspects of the autistic neurotype and identifying ways that these individuals and their families could be better accommodated and supported, he characterized the autistic community as drags on society who have nothing to contribute in a capitalistic economy. In dehumanizing autistics in this manner, he opened the door to the option of using us, once again, for human experimentation.

One of the biggest tragedies is how desperate families are being convinced to not only give their consent, but their financial assets, to participate in these studies. They are literally paying scientists to make their children human research subjects.

The Guardian highlighted how families of high-need autistic children in the US feel abandoned—because they are essentially abandoned by the system, and often left to fend for themselves. Families are often given lists from psychologists or pediatricians of needed treatments, interventions, educational supports, and sensory tools, only to find out that their insurance will not cover them. Even those who have good insurance often find that needed services and equipment are not available. It’s no wonder they are desperate to find a miracle cure.

After RFK’s speech last year, many autistic self-advocates were appalled and fearful, but many families whose children fall into the level 3 category (those needing very substantial supports) were relieved that someone in a position of power was finally talking about their struggles. The problem is that these individuals and their families don’t need untried, expensive treatments; they need affordable therapies, respite care, and adequate accommodations that they don’t have to fight for. To reference Dr. Stephen M. Shore, they need the 4 As of autism: awareness, acceptance, appreciation, and action. What we also need, Mr. Kennedy, is for you to remember that autistic people are human beings, not lab rats.

item.title: Identity and the Allure of Certainty
item.description:
Identity

Identity and the Allure of Certainty

Why embracing the unknown can set you free.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Embracing uncertainty lets us grow beyond the comforting rigidity of fixed identities.
  • Identity groups often create psychological "prisons" that limit empathy and self-evolution.
  • Rigid identities can limit human flourishing.
  • Rigorous self-examination reveals if our choices stem from genuine intent or social craving.
Source: Leeloo the First / Pexels

In her book, A Field Guide to Getting Lost, essayist Rebecca Solnit offers a beautiful piece of advice for navigating the complexities of human existence: “Leave the door open for the unknown, the door into the dark. That’s where the most important things come from.”

It is an evocative image, though we might question whether the unknown must strictly be cast in terms of darkness or light. Metaphorically, both tones carry heavy historical baggage. For many, staring straight into a blinding light is terrifying—less a symbol of enlightenment and more an invitation to a lurking migraine. Yet, the broader psychological truth remains: if we already knew the color, shape, or texture of the unknown, it wouldn’t be unknown.

Stepping away from the demand for total clarity forces us to pay closer attention to our immediate reality. As Martin Luther King Jr. famously noted during a period of immense social upheaval, “Only when it’s dark enough can you see the stars.”

Learning to sit with the unknown, and even appreciating the darker, more contemplative aspects of our internal moods, is an essential psychological skill. Unfortunately, it is a skill that is actively discouraged by our current cultural landscape.

The Tyranny of Positive Thinking

Today, we live under what can only be called the terror of toxic positivity and mandatory happiness. We treat our emotional lives as optimization problems, acting as if life shouldn’t consist of anything negative.

A major flaw in this modern obsession is that happiness is routinely sold to us as an isolated, individual achievement—a metric to be tracked on a smartwatch or secured through self-care. In reality, psychological well-being is inherently relational; it emerges from building a meaningful, shared existence alongside other people.

This need for genuine fellowship stands in stark contrast to the rigid identity politics dominating our era. Today, almost every group claims a hyper-specific, unique identity rooted in race, gender, sexuality, or religion. This constant "branding campaign" of personal identities doesn't just overshadow our deep human commonalities; it actively prevents us from making authentic connections. All identities are, fundamentally, social constructions. While they can provide a vital sense of security and belonging, they are also highly susceptible to manipulation, commercialization, and social seduction.

Unmasking Our True Intentions

To dismantle the psychological traps of rigid identity, we must first expose our underlying motives. We have to ask ourselves: What is truly impelling me toward this label? * Are you a vegetarian because of an authentic, empathetic care for the environment, or are you primarily seeking the moral status that comes with the label? Are you pursuing a prestigious career because the work itself is profoundly fulfilling, or because it is the most socially accepted path to secure public status?

When we rigorously question our motivations, we begin to understand our true intentions—the underlying drives we are consciously aware of. Friedrich Nietzsche touched on this when he wrote about the "will to power." Far from meaning a desire to dominate others, Nietzsche was referring to our innate, creative drive to actualize our potential and experience life with a sense of vitality and intensity.

This kind of psychological intensity is not a spontaneous, fleeting mood. It requires a thorough, ongoing examination of how joy and sadness function in our daily lives. We create room for who we are in the process of becoming only when we remain highly aware of what affects us, how it affects us, and for how long.

Why Identity is a Psychological Prison

The French philosopher Gilles Deleuze once pointed out a radical truth: All identities are like a prison. Regardless of how much moral goodwill or social status a specific identity grants you, it simultaneously prevents you from becoming something else—including your authentic, evolving self. The systemic danger of any identity group is that it inherently requires an "out-group" to define its "in-group." In psychological terms, a hostile "other" is almost always created alongside the friendly, protective identity. Much of the banality of human cruelty stems directly from this dualistic, us-versus-them thinking.

Nietzsche famously claimed toward the end of his life that he was "all persons in history." While his contemporaries dismissed this as a sign of mental unraveling, we might instead view it as a radical refusal to be trapped by a single, static ego.

We can describe ourselves using various professional, philosophical, or ecological labels, but true psychological freedom means acknowledging that we are also capable of empathizing with those we oppose. We are constantly in the process of dissolving old identities and becoming someone else, even if only for a fleeting moment.

From Self-Making to "Making-With"

The psychological, ecological, and social crises of our time require a fundamental shift in how we conceptualize the self. As the theorist Donna Haraway has stressed, we need to transition away from autopoiesis (isolated self-making) toward sym-poiesis (making-with).

Instead of the rigid hierarchies and constant friction that accompany fixed identities—the endless oppositions between human and nature, self and other, or us and them—our mental health relies on cultivating interdependence and proximity.

Creativity and psychological resilience rely entirely on our capacity for interconnectivity. When you truly expand your concept of the self to include other human beings and the living entities around you, rigid altruism ceases to be a chore because the world becomes a literal part of who you are. Nature is not an abstract concept "out there" to be visited; it is an active presence within us.

By replacing the drive for rigid self-branding with a philosophy of deep attention and mutual dependence, we can begin to construct a life free from the prisons of identity. In doing so, we step out of our safe, manufactured boxes and into the vast, unpredictable, and restorative space of the unknown.

item.title: Why We Pack Things We Probably Won't Need
item.description:
Cognition

Why We Pack Things We Probably Won't Need

Why "just in case" items help us stay prepared for opportunity.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • People often carry "just in case" items to preserve future opportunities, not meet current needs.
  • Research suggests humans routinely prepare for possible futures through mental simulation.
  • Everyday objects can act as reminders of valued activities, goals, and identities.
Source: Kindel Media / Pexels

When I left home on a Saturday afternoon, I slipped my laptop into my bag almost automatically. I wasn’t planning to write anything. I had coffee plans, places to be, and a reasonably full evening ahead. Yet, as I often do, I packed it “just in case.”

Minutes later, sitting on a bus with an unexpected pocket of time, I opened it and began writing.

As I typed, a question surfaced: Did I bring the laptop because I expected to use it, or did I use it simply because it was there?

The question sounds trivial, but it points to something more fundamental about how we move through the world.

Objects, or Possibilities?

Most of us regularly carry things we may never use.

A book for a journey too short to read it. A notebook that stays closed. Gym clothes that never make it to the gym. An umbrella on a clear day. A charger for a phone that still has plenty of battery.

On the surface, this can look inefficient. Why add weight for scenarios that may never happen?

Yet we do it anyway.

Because, in many cases, we are not just carrying objects. We are carrying possibilities.

The laptop in my bag is not only a device. It is a potential article, a future email, a space for an idea that might appear. A book is not just pages and ink; it is the possibility of learning something unexpected or filling an empty pause in the day.

Objects like these quietly preserve versions of ourselves we may or may not become that day.

Packing for Future Versions of Ourselves

Psychologists have long suggested that humans are uniquely capable of projecting themselves forward in time. We rehearse conversations, anticipate challenges, and mentally simulate situations that have not yet occurred.

This capacity is known as episodic future thinking—the ability to imagine ourselves in possible future scenarios (Roderer & Bohn, 2023).

When I place my laptop in my bag, I am not preparing for a specific writing session. I am preparing for a possible version of myself: The one who unexpectedly finds 20 spare minutes and decides to write.

That version of me may never show up.

But I want to be ready if it does.

The Comfort of Optionality

There is another reason we carry “just in case” items: They preserve optionality.

People tend to resist closing off potential paths, even when the likelihood of using them is small. A book preserves the option of reading. Running shoes preserve the option of exercising. A laptop preserves the option of working, creating, or learning.

The same pattern becomes especially visible when we travel. Many of us pack more than we will realistically use: extra outfits for events that may never occur, books that remain untouched, chargers that never leave the hotel room. Rationally, we know we will likely return home having used only a fraction of what we packed. Still, leaving things behind can feel oddly restrictive.

Packing, then, is not only about anticipating what will happen. It is also about protecting against what might happen. An extra outfit holds the possibility of an unexpected dinner. A novel suggests the possibility of a quiet afternoon. Running shoes hint at a version of ourselves who goes for a morning jog in a new place.

In that sense, objects act as bridges between the present and multiple possible futures.

Without the laptop, those 20 minutes on the bus would have remained empty time.

With it, they became something else entirely.

When Items Create Opportunities

We often think of opportunities as external events: a free hour appears, a meeting is cancelled, a train is delayed.

But opportunities are not only found. They are also enabled.

Source: Cottonbro / Pexels

The objects we carry shape what we notice in the first place. A spare moment feels different when a book is in your bag. A park feels different when you are wearing running shoes. A bus ride feels different when a laptop is on your lap.

Research on affordances—the possibilities for action that objects make available—suggests that our environment subtly guides what we perceive we can do (Arend & Müsseler, 2021).

In other words, carrying something doesn’t just prepare us for action. It makes certain actions more visible in the moment.

The Meaning Behind “Just in Case”

By the end of the day, I realised I had carried several items I never actually used. Yet none of them felt unnecessary.

The laptop had justified its place in my bag. But even if it hadn’t been opened, I suspect I would still have packed it again the next morning.

Because carrying “just in case” items is rarely about certainty.

It is about possibility.

We are a future-oriented species, constantly imagining what might come next and preparing for versions of ourselves that may never fully arrive. The objects we carry reflect that tendency. They are not always for the present moment. More often, they are quiet commitments to potential futures we hope might appear.

And sometimes, when those moments do arrive, we find ourselves writing an article on a bus that was never meant to be written at all.

No AI tools were used to generate the content, ideas, analysis, or authorship of this article. AI-assisted software was used solely for minor grammar and spelling checks.

item.title: The Psychology Behind Effective Leadership
item.description:
Leadership

The Psychology Behind Effective Leadership

When success becomes a leadership liability.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Past success can blind leaders to emerging risks and opportunities.
  • Challenging assumptions is essential for strategic adaptation.
  • To become a better leader, remain curious, humble, and open to change.

Success can be surprisingly dangerous.

Most of us assume that failure is what stalls careers, organizations, and leadership effectiveness. Yet, the opposite can also be true. Sometimes success itself becomes the obstacle. The habits, assumptions, and strategies that once produced positive results can gradually become barriers to future growth. Leaders who fail to recognize this paradox may find themselves hitting a ceiling—not because they lack talent, but because they continue relying on approaches that no longer fit a changing environment.

Psychology of Success and Motivational Factors
Source: Created by James Langabeer, PhD

Organizational and leadership scholars have long recognized this less obvious risk: Success can create mental shortcuts that become increasingly difficult to challenge (Argyris, 1991). The strategies that once produced positive results gradually evolve into unquestioned assumptions. What began as adaptive thinking can harden into rigid belief.

Peter Senge, author of The Fifth Discipline, argued that organizations are often constrained by deeply held "mental models"—assumptions about how the world works that become so ingrained they are rarely questioned (Senge, 1990). Over time, these mental models can limit innovation and obscure emerging threats or opportunities.

This pattern appears everywhere, from corporations and governments to healthcare organizations and personal relationships. Individuals naturally seek consistency between their past experiences and present decisions. When something works, we tend to repeat it. Seasoned executives may refer to this as "gut instinct." The problem is that environments often change faster than our beliefs do.

For leaders, this creates a paradox. The more successful someone becomes, the more likely they are to trust existing assumptions and established ways of thinking. Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman described how cognitive biases, including overconfidence and status quo bias, can lead individuals and organizations to rely excessively on familiar approaches even when circumstances have changed (Kahneman, 2011).

Leadership scholar Warren Bennis frequently emphasized that effective leaders are lifelong learners who continuously reexamine their assumptions rather than relying solely on past achievements (Bennis, 1989). Yet, many organizations reward consistency and predictability, reinforcing behaviors that once created success while discouraging experimentation and adaptation.

Ronald Heifetz's work on adaptive leadership suggests that leaders often struggle when they apply familiar solutions to fundamentally new challenges (Heifetz, 1994). In rapidly changing environments, success requires more than expertise. It requires the willingness to question established beliefs and embrace new learning.

The result is not stubbornness. It is a normal human response to uncertainty. Understanding this tendency may be one of the most important psychological challenges facing leaders today. The greatest threat to leadership effectiveness is often not a lack of knowledge, intelligence, or experience. It is becoming psychologically attached to assumptions that no longer fit reality.

The Leadership Challenge

Leaders face a difficult psychological task: distinguishing between assumptions that remain useful and those that have outlived their value. As artificial intelligence reshapes industries and organizations, the ability to learn, adapt, and rethink established beliefs may become one of leadership's most important competencies. Future success may depend less on what leaders know today and more on their willingness to question what they think they know.

Practical Ways Leaders Can Cultivate Intellectual Humility

Intellectual humility is the recognition that we may be wrong sometimes; even experienced leaders do not have all the answers. In complex environments, the willingness to learn may be more valuable than the appearance of certainty.

Leaders can strengthen intellectual humility by:

  • Questioning assumptions regularly. Ask: What are we taking for granted? And: What evidence would change our minds?
  • Seeking dissenting views. Encourage team members to challenge ideas and identify blind spots before major decisions are made.
  • Listening beyond the leadership team. Frontline employees, customers, and patients often see problems and opportunities that executives miss.
  • Conducting after-action reviews. Evaluate not only outcomes but also the assumptions that guided decisions.
  • Modeling curiosity. Be willing to admit mistakes, acknowledge uncertainty, and learn from others.

As Bennis observed, effective leaders are continuous learners. In an era of rapid change, intellectual humility may be one of the most important skills for sustaining performance and adapting strategy.

The leaders who continue to grow are not always the smartest people in the room. They are often the ones most willing to reconsider their beliefs, seek alternative perspectives, and adapt when circumstances change. In a world defined by stochastic uncertainty, adaptability begins with a simple psychological skill—questioning assumptions that once felt certain. The challenge is not merely learning something new. It is having the courage to let go of what no longer serves us.

item.title: Are You Looking After Yourself?
item.description:
Health

Are You Looking After Yourself?

Biology doesn't negotiate. Long-term wellbeing hinges on small, daily decisions.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Food and drink consumption impact the brain, mind, and body.
  • Physical activity influences neurological and neurobiological function.
  • Regular sufficient sleep is required for optimal neurobiological repair and healing.
  • Biological and neurological processes unfold according to the choices a person makes.
Source: Nils Klatt/Pixabay

"You are what you eat and drink" is not a metaphor. It is a simple reminder that your brain and body are constantly rebuilding themselves from the choices you make. Every meal and drink you consume becomes part of you.

When you choose fresh food and healthy drinks, you are giving your brain and body the kind of nourishment that is holistically beneficial. These foods and beverages provide the essential biological sustenance that helps your brain and body repair, regulate, and maintain themselves.

Fresh fruit, vegetables, whole grains, water, and a wide range of protein sources, including meat, poultry, fish, and plant‑based options such as legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas, split peas), soy foods (tofu), and nutrient‑dense seeds (almonds, walnuts, cashews, chia, and pumpkin seeds), also provide foundational nourishment for your brain and body.

These nutritional “delights” do more than satisfy hunger; they provide nourishment, flavor, and the genuine pleasure of eating food that tastes good and supports your well-being. Enjoyment and health are not opposites; with fresh food, they go hand in hand.

Carbohydrate foods are also beneficial, such as whole grains (bread, oats, rice, quinoa, barley). These carbohydrates provide fiber, micronutrients, and sustained energy essential for metabolic stability and cellular function. Altogether, these food suggestions are the kinds of foods that the body uses in its ongoing processes of growth, energy production, repair, and regulation (Becerra‑Tomás et al., 2018; Boeing et al., 2012; Chanson‑Rolle et al., 2015; Zurbau et al., 2020).

The Consensus on Healthy Eating

This is why most, if not all, international dietary guidelines generally agree on and emphasize whole fresh foods, varied plant foods, lean proteins, and minimal added sugars, sodium, and alcohol consumption. These recommendations are not abstract rules; they reflect how the brain and body successfully function.

The reason for this is that these dietary guidelines and associated food and beverage consumption also inform adverse metabolic, neurological, biological, and cardiovascular outcomes. Research consistently shows that diets built around ultra-processed foods tend to produce physiological responses that are less beneficial than those associated with fresh and minimally processed foods and healthy drinks.

Processed foods are, self-evidently, convenient and usually also taste great, but, as research shows, they often lack the natural nutritional balance found in fresh foods, including vitamins, minerals, and fiber. Over time, this biological and physiological food consumption imbalance may show up in how people feel and function (Bagnardi et al., 2015; Baliunas et al., 2009; Boeing et al., 2012; Corrao et al., 2004; Juul et al., 2022; Martínez et al., 2016; Poti et al., 2017; Schwingshackl et al., 2017; Srour et al., 2019; Zeraatkar et al., 2019).

Source: wal_172619/Pixabay

The Importance of Physical Activity

Physical activity follows the same structure. Most, if not all, international physical activity guidelines present extensive evidence showing that regular physical activity supports physical, physiological, emotional, cognitive, and psychological functioning across the lifespan (Piercy et al., 2018).

Quantitative physical activity research shows a clear pattern: When regular fitness‑focused exercise—in any form—occurs, measurable positive health and fitness benefits tend to follow. These adaptations increase the brain and body’s capacity for beneficial, sustained, holistic functional improvement (Ekelund et al., 2019; Guthold et al., 2018; Piercy et al., 2018).

Research on physical exercise and cognitive function also shows beneficial associations between physical activity and memory, executive function, and positive brain and body potential across all age groups, including older adults.

In addition to physical activity, another crucial requirement for beneficial brain and body function is the deliberate practice of getting enough sleep (Arden, 2014; Claxton, 2015; Coyle, 2009; Doidge, 2010; Doidge, 2015; Erickson et al., 2015; Suzuki, 2015).

Sleep Is Not Optional

Babies, children, teenagers, and adults all require sufficient sleep for optimal functioning because the brain and body use sleep to regulate cognition and immunity and to repair itself.

As the research indicates, when regular, acceptable, and sufficient sleep—for whatever reason—does not occur within recommended durations, adverse processes may affect cognition, attention, decision‑making, emotional regulation, and overall physical well‑being (Besedovsky et al., 2012; Diekelmann & Born, 2010; Goel et al., 2009; Krause et al., 2017; Lim & Dinges, 2010).

Immune Signaling and Sleep Duration

Research unambiguously shows that insufficient sleep also alters immune signaling and inflammatory activity. Across all ages, recommended sleep durations are well established: Children (depending on age) tend to require 10 to 14 hours of sleep; teenagers require eight to 10 hours; and adults require seven to nine hours.

These findings align with the broader neurological understanding that the brain and the body depend on restorative cycles for repair and optimal holistic beneficial functioning (Besedovsky et al., 2012; Diekelmann & Born, 2010; Goel et al., 2009; Lim & Dinges, 2010; Watson et al., 2015).

Source: Sebastian del val/Pixabay

The Brain, Mind and Body Continually Reflect Choices

Taken together, these findings reveal a broader principle: Biology does not negotiate; you are what you eat and drink, and this includes regular exercise, which plays an important part in the process.

When nutrition, exercise, and sleep are viewed together, a clear pattern emerges: The brain, mind and body is continuously responding and reflecting what a person eats and drinks, how much they move, and how much they sleep (Besedovsky et al., 2012; Doidge, 2010; Doidge, 2015; Lo et al., 2016; Medic et al., 2017; Watson et al., 2015).

What all of this is self-evidently pointing to is that you are responsible for, and have the power and control over, what you think, do, say, learn, and choose. This conscious and deliberate act of choosing fresh food, drinking healthy beverages, engaging in regular physical activity (at least three times a week for 20-30 minutes), ensuring you sleep according to recommendations, and that your choices are ethical, is not about any form of restriction; it is about your self-empowerment (Purje, 2014).

Holistic, Authentic, Enjoyable, and Sustainable Integrity

In the final analysis, this is about you—looking after yourself in a holistic, authentic, enjoyable, ethical, and sustainable way that upholds the biological integrity of the brain, mind, and body. When you look after yourself, you also tend to feel well.

And when you feel well (in terms of biological and psychological health and well-being), you can then confidently declare that you are—in terms of mind, body, and soul—looking after yourself. (Boeing et al., 2012; Kant (1785/1996); Martínez et al., 2016; Poti et al., 2017; Purje, 2014; Schwingshackl et al., 2017; Srour et al., 2019; Zeraatkar et al., 2019).

item.title: Teaching Teenagers About Love
item.description:
Adolescence

Teaching Teenagers About Love

Teens gain wisdom regarding relationships through accessing their subconscious.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Love can be expressed in different dimensions: physically, intellectually, emotionally, and spiritually.
  • Spiritual love can be thought of as connecting all living beings with each other and God.
  • Teenagers often have difficulty separating the ideas of lust and romantic love.
Source: Lilkar/Shutterstock

Part of the most hopeful work I do as a counselor involves talking with young people about what love truly is, before the world has had the chance to teach them otherwise.

When I was 15 years old, I took a summertime writing class at our local community college. One of our first assignments was, “Write about your first love.” I looked at the instructions with some dismay, because I wasn’t sure how to follow them. Did the instructor want me to write about my relationship with my mother?

Teenage years are a time of learning and increased awareness about interests, abilities, and emotions, including about romantic love. As people develop at different rates, teen experiences relating to love are quite varied, from falling in love multiple times to gaining knowledge about relationships but with no experience involving romantic feelings.

What are the Different Aspects of Love?

In discussing love with my adolescent patients and their subconscious, they have observed that love can be expressed in different dimensions: physically (including erotic attraction), intellectually, emotionally, and spiritually. My patients have noted that the emotional feeling of love intensifies when both people love each other, as opposed to one person loving another without much love given in return.

The subconscious of some of my patients have offered that spiritual love is what connects all living beings with each other and God. This is consistent with the beliefs of many of our wisdom traditions including Judaism’s concept of nitzotz, which means that there is a spark of God within each of us (Tishby, 1989), the Hindu concept of Atman, that the individual soul that is a reflection of Brahman, the universal soul or ultimate reality (Olivelle, 1998), and the Christian concept of agape, which represents love that transcends individuals and extends to all beings as an expression of divine creation (Nygren, 1953).

The Role of Touch in Expressing Love

One of my 19-year-old patients observed that he loves people and his dog intensely, but that many people have difficulty in accepting his strong feelings and desire to hug them or hold their hands. This patient was a warm and outgoing young man—an actor and dancer in a close relationship with his girlfriend—whose naturally expressive and physically affectionate temperament was not always understood or welcomed by those around him. His subconscious believed that the lack of erotic desire is the only difference between romantic and non-romantic love.

Notably, in certain cultures the non-erotic physical expression of love—such as hugging, kissing, and holding hands—are much more accepted than in Anglo-Protestant American culture. For instance, Mediterranean and Latin cultures normalize kissing on cheeks in greeting, close physical proximity, and sustained physical contact between friends of both sexes to a degree that many Americans would find uncomfortable (Hall, 1966).

I believe that American culture's touch deprivation in non-romantic contexts is unhealthy (Field, 2014). Some examples demonstrating the importance of touch in humans include that premature babies often fail to grow well or even die if they are not touched (Montagu, 1971). A mentor’s hand on the shoulder of a student can feel very supportive. In the Bible, the practice of laying on of hands was recorded as helping gain wisdom (Deut. 34:9) or healing (Mark 6:5). A hug of consolation or understanding may be healing in part through its promotion of oxytocin release that helps decrease stress (Uvnäs-Moberg, 2003).

Separating Love From Lust

Teenagers often have difficulty in separating the ideas of lust and romantic love. The subconscious of some of my patients have suggested that intense romantic involvement during adolescence can distract from other important aspects of their lives such as academic pursuits, athletics, non-romantic friendships, and vocational opportunities. However, they also acknowledge that many young people also learn significant emotional lessons through romantic relationships.

Naturally, many teenagers end up in romantic relationships that do not end happily. In part, this may be the case because young people change as they mature, and young couples often change in ways that make them incompatible in the long run. For instance, when one member of a couple decides they want a long-term relationship while the other member is not ready to make such a commitment, a breakup usually ensues.

The subconscious of one 18-year-old counseled him strongly to avoid a relationship with a particular girl whom he lusted after, because they did not have common interests. The subconscious told him that the breakup of such a relationship would cause him great discomfort. Nonetheless, my patient followed his physical feelings, got into a relationship, broke up, and felt badly.

I asked him why he chose to ignore his subconscious counsel. He responded, “I needed the experience.” This patient showed some conscious wisdom in his response in that people learn both by heeding advice and finding out things the hard way.

Takeaway: What Adolescents Can Learn About Love

The wisdom of my teenage patients and their subconscious is evident through their thoughtful ideas about love. Part of the process of maturation involves adolescents learning to take the time to consider carefully the knowledge that is accessible through interactions with their subconscious.

item.title: Why Love Makes Us Disappointed and Angry
item.description:
Relationships

Why Love Makes Us Disappointed and Angry

Our emotional inheritance drives conflict—but these steps begin to heal it.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional maturity begins with self-awareness.
  • Emotional patterns from childhood shape how people handle love and conflict as adults.
  • Love flourishes when conflict becomes an opportunity for growth.

One of the great paradoxes of intimate relationships is that the people we love often have the greatest power to hurt us. A dismissive remark from a spouse can linger in our minds for days, while a similar comment from a colleague may be forgotten within minutes. A disagreement about money, sex, or parenting can evoke emotions that seem wildly disproportionate to the issue at hand, leaving couples wondering why such ordinary conflicts become so painful and difficult to resolve.

The answer, in my experience as a couples therapist, is that intimate relationships are less about the present. They are emotional ecosystems in which our history, our insecurities, our hopes, and our unhealed wounds coexist with our love. We may believe we are arguing about household responsibilities or communication styles, but underneath the surface there are often deeper fears at work: the fear of not being important, of being rejected, controlled, abandoned, or misunderstood. Love exposes us in ways few other experiences can, and that exposure can evoke both our best qualities and our deepest vulnerabilities.

This is why I am less interested in helping couples eliminate conflict and more interested in helping them develop emotional maturity. Conflict is inevitable. Two people with different personalities, histories, and desires are bound to disappoint each other from time to time. The question is not whether conflict will arise but whether it will become an opportunity for understanding and growth, or a stage on which old wounds replay themselves.

Over the years, I have found that emotional maturity in relationships often develops through four interrelated processes: cultivating self-awareness, recognizing the emotional patterns we inherited, learning healthier ways to express difficult emotions, and eventually finding the courage to let go of old injuries that keep us trapped in cycles of resentment. These steps are not linear, and they do not promise perfection, but they offer a path toward greater intimacy and a more conscious way of loving.

Looking Inward Before Looking Outward

When couples are in distress, their attention is usually directed outward. Each partner can easily describe what the other person is doing wrong. He is emotionally unavailable. She is too critical. He withdraws. She overreacts. The list can be endless and, in many cases, not entirely inaccurate.

Yet relieving the stress rarely begins with changing the other person. It begins with understanding ourselves. It requires us to change our perception about the situation.

Self-awareness asks us to pause before reacting and become curious about our inner experience. Why does a particular comment affect me so strongly? Why do I become defensive when my partner asks for something seemingly reasonable? Why do I interpret disagreement as rejection, or emotional distance as abandonment?

The more aware we become of these internal processes, the less likely we are to mistake old pain for present reality. We begin to understand that our partner may be touching wounds they did not create, and that realization can soften blame and create room for compassion.

Self-awareness means acknowledging that we participate in the emotional dance of the relationship and that genuine change requires us to understand our own contribution to the dynamics.

Recognizing the Emotional Legacy We Bring into Love

No one enters a relationship empty-handed. We bring with us a history of experiences and a set of assumptions about what love is supposed to look like. We inherit ways of dealing with conflict, expressing anger, seeking comfort, and protecting ourselves from disappointment.

Some people learn that anger should be expressed loudly because conflict in their family was intense and dramatic. Others learn that emotions are dangerous and should be hidden because vulnerability was met with criticism or indifference. Some become caretakers, constantly attending to the needs of others while neglecting their own. Others become fiercely independent because they believe that depending on people leads to pain.

These patterns are adaptations. At one point in our lives, they may have helped us survive emotionally. The difficulty is that strategies that protected us as children often become obstacles to intimacy as adults.

Recognizing these patterns changes the conversation. Couples stop asking, "What is wrong with you?" and begin asking, "What happened to you?" or perhaps more importantly, "What did you learn about love that you are still carrying today?" This shift often transforms the emotional atmosphere in which conflict occurs. Curiosity replaces blame and accusation, and compassion becomes possible.

Learning to Express Difficult Emotions Without Destroying Connection

Many couples believe their problem is anger. More often, the problem is the inability to communicate anger and the need underneath it in ways that preserve the connection.

Anger itself is not inherently destructive. In fact, anger can be deeply informative. It tells us that something matters to us, that a boundary has been crossed, or that an important need is not being met. The challenge is learning to communicate these experiences without attacking, blaming, or controlling the other person.

This is particularly difficult because criticism is often easier than vulnerability. It feels safer to say, "You never listen," than to admit, "I feel lonely, and I miss feeling close to you." It feels easier to accuse someone of selfishness than to reveal our fear of not mattering.

Healthy relationships require the courage to speak from our own experience with kindness. They ask us to describe our feelings without assuming malicious intent, to express disappointment without contempt, and to remain connected to our vulnerability even when anger feels justified.

It requires practice and a willingness to tolerate discomfort. It asks us to relinquish the desire to win arguments and replace it with the aspiration to understand and be understood.

Letting Go of Old Hurts

Perhaps the hardest work in relationships is not learning how to communicate or manage conflict. It is learning how to let go.

Some injuries remain alive long after the original event has passed. A betrayal, a rejection, a period of emotional neglect, or years of feeling unseen can leave scars that shape the way we relate to ourselves and to others. Without realizing it, we begin to organize our lives around protecting ourselves from being hurt again.

The problem is that protection and intimacy are often at odds with one another. When we cling to resentment, we remain emotionally attached to the very pain we wish to escape. We become suspicious, guarded, and hypervigilant. We expect disappointment and unknowingly create distance in an attempt to avoid future suffering. Letting go is a decision to stop allowing past injuries to dictate our present relationships.

This process takes time. It requires grieving what was lost, accepting what cannot be changed, and developing the courage to remain open despite uncertainty. Yet without this work, intimacy becomes nearly impossible because love cannot flourish in a heart that is permanently preparing for battle.

Love Requires Courage

Mature love requires emotional courage, the courage to know ourselves honestly, to question old patterns, to communicate vulnerably, and to release resentments that no longer serve us.

Relationships ask for awareness. They ask for humility. They ask us to acknowledge that we are all works in progress. Love is the willingness to use conflict as an invitation to grow. When couples approach their struggles with curiosity rather than certainty, with compassion rather than blame, and with courage rather than defensiveness, something remarkable happens. The relationship becomes more than a source of comfort or companionship. It becomes a place of transformation.

And perhaps that is one of the greatest gifts of intimate relationships: They challenge us not merely to love another person, but to become more fully ourselves in the process.

item.title: Why Your Brain Assumes the Worst
item.description:
Anxiety

Why Your Brain Assumes the Worst

The stories your brain tells aren't always true—but you can rewrite them.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Your brain is wired to fill uncertainty with worst-case scenarios.
  • Negativity bias makes one bad possibility outweigh many good ones.
  • Creating multiple explanations can build a more hopeful brain.

Have you ever sent a text and then checked your phone after five minutes?

Or 10?

Or 30?

Once the hour is over, you are more than curious about the lack of response; you have made up your mind. You think, "They must be mad at me," "I should not have said that," or "I have ruined our relationship."

Or, perhaps you are walking through the office and see a coworker walk by without saying hello, or your supervisor sends you an email and does not write much in it, or when you are at lunch with a friend, they are quieter than usual.

Unconsciously, your brain fills in the blank; when you experience uncertainty, you are usually not uncertain for long; you believe you are being rejected.

What is surprising is that this is not an indication that you are insecure or oversensitive but, rather, a reflection of your brain functioning as it is supposed to.

Your Brain Is Designed to Keep You in a Group

For our ancestors to survive, it was more than just nice to not be alone and be part of a group; it was critical for their survival. When they were excluded from a group, consequences could be dire.

This means our brains have developed to be very sensitive to social cues and to constantly look for cues in the environment that we are part of a group with others and that we are valued and connected with others.

Research has shown that social rejection activates many of the same neural systems that activate physical pain (Eisenberger et al., 2003). Our need to belong and to connect with one another is not simply an emotional need; it is also a biological need.

Your Brain Dislikes Uncertainty

Although anxiety is often described as being caused by experiencing negative events, incomplete information can cause increased anxiety levels, too.

If enough pieces of information aren't available to complete the puzzle for you, your brain will try to find those missing pieces on its own. Unfortunately, it does a terrible job of doing this because when it generates assumptions about missing information, it generates negative assumptions (due to evolutionary reasons). Our ancestors, who thought there was a greater possibility of danger than there really was, most likely had a better chance of surviving.

Let's say you've emailed someone and they haven't replied yet. There could be many reasons for this, such as:

  • They can't respond because they're too busy.

  • Their phone is out of battery.

Instead of reasoning with the above possibilities, anxious people reason with just one possibility.

  • "They may not like me anymore."

This is not an opinion formed because there is any evidence supporting it, but rather because when we lack certainty, we will have an uncomfortable feeling.

Negativity Is the Default Setting for Your Brain

Your brain, by default, assigns more weight to experiences with negative elements when recalling them than to those with positive aspects (Baumeister et al., 2001).

You may have 20 instances of positive interactions throughout each day, but if you have one negative instance and only a short email or missed greeting, that is the instance your brain will continue to focus on.

In our modern life, however, it can create unnecessary suffering.

Creating a More Hopeful Brain

According to Snyder's Hope Theory (Snyder 2002), hopeful people generate multiple pathways around obstacles rather than becoming trapped by a single dead end. In relationships, that means creating multiple explanations before accepting the one fear gives you.

Whenever your mind jumps to the worst-case scenario, take a moment before you accept its first version of events as fact.

To do this, write down what your brain came up with in the moment. (Example: They haven't replied because they are mad at me.)

Next, write down three other possible explanations that would fit all the same evidence. (For example: They were in a meeting, they are busy, or they saw the text but plan to reply later.)

Finally, one of the three alternatives must be something positive. Why? Because our brains have evolved to be biased toward the negative, and we can get stuck in the negative hole when we only have one version of events to go by. As we’ve evolved, when we assume that danger is present, we have a better chance of surviving.

Hope is the practice of intentionally thinking differently. By allowing for and creating a positive possibility, we are not lying to ourselves about how bad or scary things are; we are giving our brains one example of what happens when we balance out their natural imbalance.

After you have written out the three possibilities (one of which must be positive), ask yourself, “Which one of these is based on evidence and which one of these is based on fear?”

You will never be able to confirm which explanation of the two (or more) possibilities is correct, so understanding that is not the goal.

Hope increases as we create multiple possibilities for overcoming barriers to our goals. In this case, the barrier is the assumption about another person's silence.

Each time you practice creating alternatives, you increase your flexibility in your thought processes, and you continue to reduce the power of negativity bias. Over time, your brain will make an association and stop asking, "Why does that always happen to me?" and begin to ask, "What else could be correct?"

Hope isn't believing the best-case scenario. Hope is refusing to believe the worst-case scenario is the only one.

item.title: What Blue Zones Can Teach Us About Happiness
item.description:
Happiness

What Blue Zones Can Teach Us About Happiness

What the world's happiest and healthiest communities get right.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • A strong sense of purpose is linked to greater well-being and health.
  • Close relationships consistently predict happiness and flourishing.
  • Joyful movement and savoring everyday moments support life satisfaction.

As a psychology professor, I teach a large undergraduate course called "The Science of Happiness." In the class, we explore positive psychology, the scientific study of how to live “the good life.”

While mental health conversations often focus on anxiety, depression, and other challenges, positive psychology is concerned with what helps people build fulfilling, meaningful, and joyful lives.

My favorite part of teaching this course is that we don’t just talk about positive psychology; we practice it.

Throughout the semester, my students complete experiential assignments based on research-backed happiness-boosting strategies. These activities include identifying their values, practicing gratitude, cultivating positive relationships, engaging in acts of kindness, and finding forms of movement they genuinely enjoy.

This summer, I have the opportunity to teach a study abroad version of the course in Okinawa, Japan.

Okinawa is famous for being one of the world's "Blue Zones," regions where people tend to live longer, healthier, and happier lives than almost anywhere else on Earth. The other blue zones are Sardinia, Italy; Ikaria, Greece; Nicoya, Costa Rica, and Loma Linda, California.

While there is no single secret to Okinawan longevity or happiness, many aspects of daily life there align remarkably well with the principles I teach in my class.

But you don’t need to live in one of these places to reap the benefits. Here are a few Okinawa-inspired happiness practices worth borrowing.

Find Your Ikigai

One of Japan’s most famous concepts is ikigai, which roughly translates to "a reason to get up in the morning."

Research consistently shows that having a sense of purpose is associated with better psychological well-being and even physical health. What brings purpose to your life is unique to you. It might be raising your children, mentoring younger colleagues, creating art, serving your community, or pursuing meaningful work.

When we get caught up in the hustle of our busy lives, it’s easy to lose sight of what truly matters to you.

Invest in Your Relationships

One factor that consistently emerges as an important predictor of happiness is a strong sense of social connection.

In Okinawa, people often belong to close-knit social groups known as moai, networks of friends who provide support, companionship, and practical help throughout life.

article continues after advertisement

Move Because You Enjoy It

Many Americans approach exercise as a to-do list task. Okinawans treat movement differently.

Rather than relying on intense workouts at a gym, movement is woven into daily life through walking, gardening, household tasks, and community activities.

Research shows that physical activity improves mood and well-being, and we're much more likely to stick with it when it feels enjoyable and meaningful rather than obligatory.

Slow Down Enough to Notice What's Good

One thing that strikes many visitors to Japan is the attention paid to everyday experiences. This might look like appreciating seasonal changes, savoring a meal, or enjoying a beautiful view

Positive psychology research tells us that people who intentionally savor positive experiences tend to experience greater well-being than those who rush through them.

You don’t have to take a vacation or plan an epic event to notice the good. Instead, slow down and mindfully observe what’s already there.

Happiness Is Built Through Practice

As a busy professor and parent, it's one thing for me to teach evidence-based happiness strategies. It's another thing to consistently practice them myself.

That's one reason I'm excited about this trip. Over the next three weeks, I'll be encouraging my students (and myself) to step outside of our usual routines and experiment with the habits that support flourishing.

I’m hoping that, by being surrounded by a culture that supports these practices, we can build happiness habits to bring home with us.

item.title: The Forgotten History of Amphetamine Psychosis
item.description:
Psychosis

The Forgotten History of Amphetamine Psychosis

Recovering the hidden past of medications used to treat ADHD and psychosis risk.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • A 2024 study revealed a clear association between certain ADHD medications and psychosis.
  • The phenomenon of amphetamine-induced psychosis was known since the 1950s.
  • Psychiatry repeatedly loses sight of this well-documented side effect of amphetamine-based ADHD drugs.

In 2024, a highly publicized study in the American Journal of Psychiatry (Moran et al. 2024) showed that people taking drugs like Adderall for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) were more than five times more likely to experience psychosis.

At high clinical doses (around 30 mg of dextroamphetamine, or 40 mg Adderall), amphetamine-based drugs were associated with hallucinations and persecutory delusions. The study estimates that 81 percent of such cases could have been avoided at lower doses.

Source: Towfiqu barbhuiya / Pexels

The study didn’t just find a risk at very high doses. Even those taking moderate doses have a higher likelihood of developing psychosis compared to people not taking them.

The media treated the study as a shocking, even scandalous, discovery. Psychiatrists were quick to assure the public that such side effects are rare. But the link between amphetamines and psychosis isn’t new. It is one of the oldest findings in modern psychiatry.

In 1967, a doctor even used amphetamines to deliberately induce psychosis in ordinary volunteers.

So how do we keep forgetting this lesson? And how can knowing its history help us shape the future?

Discovering Amphetamine Psychosis

Amphetamine psychosis was first named by the British doctor P. H. Connell in 1953. A patient came to London’s Maudsley Hospital experiencing hallucinations, delusions, and paranoia. He was hearing voices and convinced that his boss wanted to murder him over a patent dispute.

Connell admitted him to the hospital with a diagnosis of schizophrenia. A few days later, the symptoms were gone. A careful follow‑up revealed that his psychosis had been induced by large quantities of amphetamines. (At the time, one could purchase amphetamines over the counter as a decongestant.)

Connell wondered if any other doctors had reported this strange side effect of amphetamines. He began to ask his colleagues and dig through case files. He thought he might find three or four cases in the medical literature.

He found 42.

He was appalled that the link between amphetamines and psychosis was not more widely known. He wrote a book called Amphetamine Psychosis to document his findings. He argued in the British Medical Journal for sharper restrictions on their sale.

But Connell’s demands were largely ignored. The problem was that amphetamines were considered a wonder drug on par with penicillin. By the 1940s, amphetamines were prescribed for fatigue, narcolepsy, ADHD, weight loss, and depression. Amphetamines, doctors claimed, could even restore a certain “zest” to life for bored housewives and jaded businessmen.

Nobody wanted to think of them as a pill that could make you mad.

The Quest to Create Insanity

Amphetamine psychosis was rediscovered in the late 1960s due to an epidemic of injectable amphetamine use in the United States.

In the early 1960s, doctors in Southern California wanted to help heroin users get clean by prescribing methamphetamine vials. They thought that injecting amphetamine would be safer and less addictive.

That misjudgment created a large subculture of intravenous amphetamine users—the so-called “Speed Freaks.” They would often develop hallucinations and paranoid delusions. Speed users were regularly showing up at mental hospitals, often misdiagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia.

One doctor became so fascinated by the link between amphetamines and psychosis that he tried to induce psychosis in normal volunteers. He believed that a pill that could reliably create a schizophrenia-like state would benefit mental health research.

He gathered a group of four volunteers—recreational speed users—and gave them amphetamine tablets until they became psychotic. This experiment demonstrated that amphetamines could induce psychosis in people with no prior history of mental illness. His experiment also gave rise to the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia, which transformed psychiatry in the 1970s.

The link between amphetamine use and psychosis was briefly rediscovered in the late 1980s, thanks to a paper in the Journal of Emergency Medicine that documented 127 cases (Derlet et al. 1989). The authors noted that such patients were frequently misdiagnosed because doctors did not realize the psychosis was linked to amphetamine use.

A Forgotten Lesson

So, why do we keep forgetting this lesson? Why was it such a shock when the 2024 article revealed a connection between amphetamine-based drugs like Adderall and psychosis?

One reason is that although doctors knew amphetamines could cause psychosis, they believed this occurred mainly in people who abused amphetamines by taking large doses—far larger than those prescribed for conditions like ADHD.

As long as people were taking clinically approved doses, as judged by their doctor, they were not expected to experience psychosis.

I suspect that another reason was the exact one that P. H. Connell encountered: Nobody wants to think we’re collectively exposing young people to a psychosis risk. In 2022, about 7 million American children were diagnosed with ADHD; that’s about one in 10 kids. About half of them are on medication.

So what does this mean? Does this mean that nobody should take drugs like Adderall? No, not at all. Adderall can certainly be beneficial for some people at some stages of their lives.

But it does mean that we should stop treating amphetamine‑induced psychosis as a shocking anomaly and start recognizing it as a well‑documented risk—one psychiatry has discovered, forgotten, and rediscovered for 70 years.

This post was adapted from my book, The Madness Pill: One Doctor’s Quest to Understand Schizophrenia (St. Martin’s Press, 2026).

item.description:
Forensic Psychology

Faking Insanity: How Experts Tell What's Real

The insanity defense looks like a legal loophole. It isn't.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Faking insanity is real. So is branding a genuinely insane person a liar.
  • You can be genuinely ill and still exaggerate.
  • Being clearly psychotic isn't enough to win. There must be a link between the symptoms and the crime.

On October 30, 2012, in Naperville, Illinois, 40-year-old Elzbieta Plackowska stabbed her 7-year-old son and a 5-year-old girl she was babysitting. She told evaluators she had been hearing voices. The psychiatrist retained by her defense concluded she was in the grip of a manic episode and could not appreciate that what she had done was wrong.

The psychiatrist called by the prosecution wasn’t buying it. Her story kept shifting. She said the children had seen the same visions she did, but real hallucinations don’t work that way. And the voices, she said, had spoken to her in English, though her first language was Polish. After a bench trial in 2017, the judge sided with the prosecution and convicted her.

Two forensic psychiatrists examined the same woman and reached opposite conclusions about whether she was lying. Cases like this turn on one of the hardest judgments in forensic work: whether a defendant who claims to be mentally ill is telling the truth. The fear of being fooled by a faker is real. The opposite mistake is just as costly: branding a sick person a liar. The error cuts both ways.

It Looks Like an Easy Out. It Rarely Is.

Ask the average juror, and you will hear that the insanity defense is a common loophole, easy to fake, and used all the time to dodge punishment. Decades of research say otherwise: Insanity pleas are rare, seldom succeed, and usually end in long psychiatric confinement, not release.

But the fear that a dangerous person will be set free to run amok in the community isn’t unfounded. Faking insanity happens. A 2025 analysis of roughly 1,300 people in a forensic psychiatry practice found that about a quarter failed at least three tests designed to catch invented or exaggerated symptoms.

Psychosis Shows Up at 3 a.m.

A validity measure tests whether someone is reporting honestly and putting in real effort. Some flag the person who reports too many dramatic, rare, or impossible mental health symptoms. Others track effort on tasks that look hard but are easy enough that even brain-injured patients pass. A deliberately poor score stands out.

The tests catch a lot. So does the conversation. With someone who is genuinely sick, you don’t just hear about the symptoms; you see them. They stop mid-sentence to listen to a voice no one else can hear. Their fear matches the paranoid delusion. A faker can describe all of that, but can’t produce it.

In nearly 30 years of competency and criminal responsibility evaluations, I’ve found that the genuinely ill rarely perform their illness. They’re too busy living inside it. It’s the performers who hand you the symptoms in the order a movie taught them.

Some defendants will agree to almost any symptom you ask them about. Some don’t even know what a hallucination is, mistaking something ordinary, like talking to themselves, for one. Others overdo it, piling on incompatible symptoms that no real illness produces: the wired, sleepless high of mania running full blast next to the dead weight of deep depression, hour after hour. That isn’t how illness works.

And the interview is only part of it. Listening to jail call recordings can be enlightening; despite clear indications that these calls are recorded, you'd be amazed at what some defendants reveal. Some of the most valuable sources are the officers and nurses who staff the jail, who are around the defendant for hours with no skin in the game. They see the defendant at three in the morning and in the lunch line. A performance is exhausting to sustain around the clock, and it often slips when the audience no longer matters.

When a Hunch Becomes Expert Testimony

The defense has its own legitimate worry. Law professor Deborah Denno recently tracked malingering claims across every American insanity case involving neuroscience evidence over the past 120 years. The accusation grew from a rarity in the early 1900s to more than a fifth of insanity cases by the 2000s. When it was raised, it shaped the outcome in roughly 70 percent of cases.

Yet much of the time it rested on thin support. Often, the finding came down to an examiner’s impression that the defendant seemed manipulative. Not a failed test, not a validity measure, but a feeling about the person across the table, written up in clinical language and carried into a courtroom as expertise.

None of this means faking isn't real. It is, and modern tests can catch it. The trouble is that the courtroom malingering accusation, all too often, doesn't include them. It rests on a clinician's gut read, the same blunt hunch the field ran on a century ago, before those tests existed. The science got sharp. The accusation often didn't. And it can carry a case without anyone running the assessment that might have settled it.

Spotting a Liar Is a Coin Toss

It’s tempting to think you’d know a faker if you saw one. The research says otherwise. Across hundreds of studies and more than 20,000 observers, the average person spots a lie about 54 percent of the time, barely better than a coin toss. We psychologists only do a smidgen better. And here's an interesting fact: How confident you feel about your judgment has almost nothing to do with whether you’re right.

It’s why I don’t lean on my own impression of a defendant, and why I’m wary of any examiner who does. The face across the table is the least reliable instrument in the room.

When that certainty hardens into a courtroom opinion, someone pays. In a New York case, a young woman named Keila Pulinario shot a man she said had raped her and intended to do it again. The state’s psychiatrist called her a faker. At trial, she admitted she had lied to the evaluators about her sexual history, and the judge used those lies to bar her own expert from explaining her trauma to the jury. A federal court reversed, holding that her untruthfulness was a symptom of what she had survived, not a reason to silence her defense. Withholding and shame are not holes in a rape victim’s account. They are part of it.

Two Ways to Be Fooled

Mistaking a sick person for a faker denies them treatment and adds years to a sentence. Mistaking a faker for a sick person lets a fabrication corrupt the verdict. Both are real dangers, and both come from the same shortcut: trusting a feeling instead of doing the work, watching how the symptoms show up, running the tests built to catch a fake, and checking the story against the people who see the defendant when no one is performing for a judge. The difference between a genuine breakdown and a good act is there to be found. What hides it is an examiner who has already made up their mind.
